#8206. The Glacier Died—And the Trail Runners Started Coming

I’m standing with Samuel Mendoza on top of Chacaltaya Mountain, 17,785 feet above sea level. Under our feet is a sharp slope of scree, a jumbled descent of rocks with patches of snow. The air is thin, and the vast Bolivian landscape surrounds us.

Directly ahead, the Altiplano—the high plain—stretches from the foot of the mountain. El Alto, the chaotic concrete and red brick city that has grown to roughly 900,000 people, lies at the far edge of the plain at 13,000 feet of elevation, crammed against a canyon’s edge. About 1,500 feet below and connected by a series of cable cars, La Paz, Bolivia’s seat of government, sprawls.

Behind us rises the Huayna Potosí massif. The nearly 20,000-foot summit towers above, its glaciated peak passing in and out of fast-moving clouds. About 45 miles to the northwest, Lake Titicaca—the central motif to Inca creation stories—shimmers on the horizon.

It’s here, on this high mountain of almost-bare rock cradled in the Andes, that Mendoza learned to ski.

Located roughly 20 miles north of La Paz, Chacaltaya was once the world’s highest-altitude ski resort. It began in the 1930s when Raúl Posnansky, an engineer and ski enthusiast, recognized the mountain’s potential, according to 2023 reporting by “Radio Ambulante.” Chacaltaya’s glacier, though relatively small in area at roughly 55 acres, was a solid tongue of ice descending the slope. Temperatures up high stayed low, and snow fell heavily and often during the wet season. The ice was there, had always been there, and would always be there, by all indications at the time.

Posnansky worked to materialize his skiing fantasy: He hired laborers to build an access road, haul materials, construct cabins, and install the first rope tow at Chacaltaya—powered by a truck engine housed in a cabin hanging over the base of the ski run.

Posnansky, along with other mountain athletes, founded the Club Andino Boliviano, a group of dedicated skiers and enthusiasts. To fund the growing ski scene, the club drew involvement from La Paz’s middle and upper classes, and Posnansky and the club persuaded Bolivia’s Congress to pass tax legislation dedicating 1% of the country’s hotel revenue to Bolivia’s Ski and Mountaineering Federation. This funding would help transform Chacaltaya from a passion project into the hub of Bolivian skiing—a hub that, while retaining its roughshod, backyard roots, would grow to host a national ski team, crowded weekend races, the first South American ski championships, and athletes who would represent the country at Winter Olympics.

When Mendoza was a young boy in El Alto, his family wasn’t connected to La Paz’s urban elite who would drive across the Altiplano to ski. Mendoza’s father, however, worked as the caretaker of Chacaltaya, often living for weeks at a time at the resort to maintain the facilities.

When he was 15, Mendoza accompanied his father to the mountain for the first time. He spent his first night at the base racked by altitude sickness.

“My dad gave me coca leaf tea,” he says. The next day, “the sun came out; I felt better. I got acclimated, and I learned to ski.”

Fifty years later, standing once again on the summit, Mendoza is transported back to the resort’s heyday.

“The rope would drop us off here,” he says. “And then …” He puts his hands on bent knees and waves them back and forth in a slalom. He raises his hands over his head and lets out a high yell, feeling the old rush of racing in the cold air.

Mendoza is in his 60s now. He has a harder time seeing, looking out through thick glasses, and his knees sometimes bother him.

Around us the glacier has completely vanished, leaving behind only a mountain of rock.

Infatuated with the world of snow and slopes, Mendoza learned to ski on gear borrowed from Club Andino. He worked long, physical days with his father, tasks ranging from construction and upkeep to manning the rope tow—including rebraiding the wire cable whenever it snapped, a job that left Mendoza with thin white scars across his fingers. From his father, he learned to manage the mountain, the two often sleeping in the lodge for weeks at a time.

Meanwhile, his love for skiing only deepened. Mendoza remembers Stanley Shepard, an American diplomat posted in Bolivia, who taught him advanced techniques and shared the joy of the mountain.

“Stan would drive up this road so fast,” he says as we drive the same route from the city to Chacaltaya some 50 years later. He smiles with the memory of the adrenaline rush.

Mendoza’s ski story exists in a split reality: In one, he is the caretaker’s son, surrounded by a country’s elites who lived near, but not next to, families like his. The socioeconomic divide paralleled the geography: La Paz’s wealthy neighborhoods in the valley, El Alto on the cold outcropping of the Altiplano above. Despite the divide, Mendoza was a vital member of the Chacaltaya scene; the members of Club Andino were his friends. The nights were full of music whenever others would sleep alongside him and his father at the refugio. The period is marked in Mendoza’s mind by shared meals in the cabin and shared runs on the mountain.

By the 1970s, with Chacaltaya entering its golden period, Mendoza was both employee and skier. He tells me he used to set up for the weekend slalom races—ones he’d often compete in as well. I ask about the slalom poles, curious about infrastructure. He tells me they were made nearby. “But the first times,” he says, “we used hollow canes, like cornstalks.”

In a 1976 article in Ski Magazine, American writer Jeff Frees described his visit to the ski hill. There were some two dozen weekly skiers sharing the piste and “a slightly doglegged swath of snow” that was “lined with rocks from top to bottom,” although there were no lift lines, he writes.

The chalet, perched on a rocky precipice, was “so frightening and insecure-looking,” that “some skiers refused to enter it,” Frees says. With the altitude nearing 18,000 feet, other visitors didn’t even bother trying, exiting the minibus up from La Paz only to climb into the truck heading back down the road.

This was the electric, eclectic golden period. One 1,000-foot run served by a single rope tow prone to snapping and powered by a truck engine. A handful of foreign visitors and the dedicated group of Club Andino members. A small, warm refugio built on a cliffside, filled with coca tea, quinoa soup, and music. Weekend races and training events for young locals, supporting ski teams who would go on to participate in four consecutive Olympics starting in 1980. And behind this incredible scene was Samuel Mendoza.

“It was frozen all the time,” Mendoza says. “The people said, ‘This is forever. It will never recede.’”

“But little by little, it started to thaw.”

Scientists had been documenting Chacaltaya for decades, but a systematic study of the glacier began in 1991, led in part by Edson Ramírez of the Universidad Mayor de San Andrés in La Paz (UMSA). Glaciologists’ observations began to echo the concerns skiers had voiced for years: Chacaltaya was melting—and fast.

“Snow would fall at night,” Mendoza says, “but it would be gone by midday.” As temperatures rose, the glacier retreated, exposing more and more of the rock underneath.

While the retreat was evident in some of the earliest photos from the 1940s, Ramírez and his team found that, in just six years from 1992 to 1998, the glacier’s melt had accelerated dramatically, losing more than 40% of its surface area and roughly two-thirds of its ice volume. The team’s prediction: The glacier would disappear within 10 to 15 years.

By 2009, the glacier was completely gone.

“The entire glacier of the world’s highest ski slope had turned to water,” Mendoza reflects.

As the ski run melted under them, various last-ditch efforts were implemented to keep the sport alive. Artificial snow production was attempted, but ultimately proved too costly. Moving the resort to other nearby mountains was considered, but transportation and access were constant hurdles. Even traditional Andean rituals were offered to the mountain gods.

But the glacier, once gone, would not come back.

Without their ski hub, the Club Andino eventually unraveled. A photo hangs in the abandoned refugio of smiling members piled outside the club. Mendoza tells me their names—a running list of friends moved abroad or passed away. Even their headquarters in La Paz is now shuttered.

While sooner than expected, Chacaltaya’s glacier death was not unique within the broader scope of Andean glaciers. Research published in 2026 by Giuliana Adrianzen and Andrew Malone of the University of Illinois Chicago found that Bolivia’s Cordillera Real lost a stunning 42% of its glaciated area between 1992 and 2024.

This trend is widespread across the Andes, which are home to 99% of the world’s tropical glacier area—particularly vulnerable ice fields located near the Earth’s equator.

Glaciers in this latitudinal band are much more susceptible to small temperature changes than those outside of it. Kept frozen primarily by extreme altitude, tropical glaciers already exist close to the temperature threshold to sustain permanent ice; they also don’t experience the long, cold winters of glaciers nearer the poles. Andean glaciers are now thinning 35% faster than the global average, according to a 2025 international report co-authored by researchers at the University of Sheffield. As global warming pushes the freezing level higher, more precipitation falls on these glaciers as rain instead of snow, accelerating the melt.

Over the 60 years between 1960 and 2020, Peru lost 56% of its glacier area. In 2024, Venezuela was declared glacier-free with the death of the Humboldt Glacier (named, perhaps ominously, after the German naturalist who pioneered the notion that everything in the natural world is connected). Colombia is following the same trajectory, having lost more than 90% of its glaciated area since the mid-1800s.

According to UNESCO, the Andes could lose 78 to 97% of their tropical glacier volume by the year 2100.

Of course, more than skiing is at risk—including the water supply risk of some 90 million people across the Andes. These glaciers serve as water reserves for the millions of people who live downstream, and their disappearance foreshadows looming ecological disasters. Many Andean municipalities also rely on hydroelectric power, which depends on steady dry-season meltwater from the glaciers. As the glaciers shrink, that flow is dwindling, increasing the severity of droughts.

While Chacaltaya’s lift has long since stopped spinning, a handful of trained guides and foreign clients continue to practice ski mountaineering in Bolivia, climbing high peaks and bombing descents on still-intact glaciers. While the chalet has ceased to function, the mountain remains an active scientific base. The Chacaltaya Observatory, run by UMSA’s Laboratory for Atmospheric Physics—with multiple international collaborators—continues to measure the atmosphere, climate, and cosmic rays.

And although skiing has abandoned the mountain, Mendoza has not.

Since his father died on Chacaltaya over 30 years ago, Mendoza has served as the mountain’s main caretaker, a position he continues to hold. He spends more time in El Alto with his family now, but he and his brother Adolfo still make multiple trips a week to Chacaltaya, welcoming the handful of tourists who come to visit the abandoned chalet or use it as an acclimatization hike. With the small collected entrance fees, he pays for repairs and maintains his memories of the resort.

Many of Mendoza’s days, however, are spent in solitude, standing alone at 17,000 feet on Chacaltaya’s rocky remains.

“When you’re alone it’s a little sad,” he says. “With only the birds, the condors, the Andean foxes.”

Since the collapse of the glacier, a new group of athletes has taken to Chacaltaya: trail runners—whose arrival is directly tied to skiing’s disappearance. Paolo Choque is the director of skyrunning for the Bolivian Ski and Mountaineering Federation. One of the “last people to learn to ski in Bolivia,” Choque witnessed the collapse of skiing at Chacaltaya, and he has since helped cultivate trail running to take its place.

In 2001, when Choque learned to ski, the main chunk of the glacier was already “ruined,” he says. Against the backdrop of the dying mountain, Choque became involved in promoting skiing and snowboarding in Bolivia, including searching for alternative mountains to host competitions.

In 2011, the federation found another suitable slope at nearby Charquini and hosted a Bolivian Ski Championship. Choque says that snowboarding grew in popularity over a handful of years with the promotion efforts, but participation numbers remained low—with just 25 racers in the snowboard event in 2015. Amid melting ice and low participation, he made the decision to pivot. “I said, ‘No, this isn’t going anywhere. We don’t even have a ski slope.’”

Inspired by the sport’s explosion in Spain, Choque organized a pilot skyrunning race on Chacaltaya in 2016, which was met with a strong reception. Athletes had returned to the mountain. The federation’s championship now draws about 200 participants each year, according to Choque. Racers gain points at multiple events across the country, which take place over otherworldly terrain—from the world’s largest salt flats in Uyuni to the folds of the Sajama stratovolcano, the shores of Lake Titicaca, and, of course, Chacaltaya Mountain.

“Skiing may have died,” Choque says, “but mountain sports have not.”

While private trail races have also increased in popularity in Bolivia over the past decade, the federation aims to develop skyrunning and its next generation of athletes through accessible competition. Race entries, Choque emphasizes, are kept inexpensive, and youth competition categories give athletes the opportunity to qualify for international competition.

“For me, sport must come first, and it must be accessible to everyone,” Choque says.

Despite challenges with funding, Choque says the federation has seen success in sending participants to compete in the South American Championships, where they have earned podium finishes, including three medals in 2025.

As one sport fades and another grows, Choque defines what success could look like for Bolivian skyrunning.

“What I want to achieve is to bring a South American championship here, and if possible, even a youth world championship to Bolivia,” he says. “We have the potential.”

Paolo and the federation hope that Chacaltaya will continue to be an important mountain hub for decades to come—with or without the glacier.

For all of the uniqueness of Chacaltaya’s history, it does mirror a larger global skiing trend: most of the participants were wealthy. Mendoza remembers well the divide caused by the cost of equipment. “From the city of El Alto there weren’t a lot of skiers,” he says.

Through the Ski and Mountaineering Federation, Choque is determined that the next iteration of Chacaltaya’s mountain sports—trail and sky running—do not follow the same pattern. Mendoza, meanwhile, has seen some of the runners who are taking to the mountain to train where he once skied. I ask him if he would ever run one of the races, and he tells me he enjoys running. His knees, though, keep him from doing too much of it. But when a German tourist wanted to race from the summit to the lagoon below, Mendoza happily said yes.

“Replacing skiing at Chacaltaya in the future is possible,” he says.

Looking across the dry slope where he learned to ski, the rusted remains of his rope tow, the faded chalet and the memories contained, Mendoza takes a deep breath. At the end of the day, as we drive the winding dirt road down to the city with Chacaltaya shrinking into the distance behind us, he looks ahead.

“It makes me happy when people visit the mountain,” he says.

#8204. These Ski Resorts Let You Ski for Free on the Day You Arrive

November 28, 2023; Bozeman, MT, USA; Horizon Airlines operations at Bozeman Yellowstone International Airport (BZN). Mandatory Credit: Joe Nicholson-Alaska Airlines (Photo: Courtesy of Alaska Airlines)

A ski vacation usually starts with a travel day. Between catching flights, collecting luggage, and making your way to the mountains, it’s easy to lose an entire day before you ever click into your skis. But what if you could hit the slopes the same day you land, without paying for a lift ticket?

While free arrival-day skiing might sound too good to be true, it’s not a new concept. Park City, Utah, previously offered a program called Quick START, which allowed travelers flying into Salt Lake City International Airport to exchange their same-day boarding pass for a complimentary lift ticket at Park City Mountain Resort, Deer Valley Resort, or Canyons Resort. Although the program has since ended, the idea of turning a travel day into a ski day hasn’t disappeared.

Today, several ski resorts and airlines offer similar incentives. Some require flying with a specific airline, while others are available to travelers booking an eligible resort stay.

Through its Atmos Rewards Alpine Getaways program, Alaska Airlines partners with ski destinations across the western United States and Canada to offer travelers special perks. For the 2026–’27 season, the airline has confirmed partnerships with Crystal Mountain in Washington and Palisades Tahoe in California, with additional resorts potentially joining as the season progresses.

In previous seasons, the airline has also partnered with Alyeska Resort, Arctic Valley Ski Area, and Eaglecrest Ski Area in Alaska; Bogus Basin and Schweitzer in Idaho; Jackson Hole Mountain Resort in Wyoming; and Sun Peaks Resort in British Columbia.

While some participating resorts have offered complimentary lift tickets, others have provided discounted rentals and additional perks. At Palisades Tahoe, travelers can present a same-day Alaska Airlines or Hawaiian Airlines boarding pass or proof of Atmos Rewards membership to access the resort’s offer. Details for Crystal Mountain’s 2026–2’7 promotion are still being finalized.

“Skiing is a natural fit for Alaska because we serve so many great mountain destinations across the West,” Sarah Lasky, Senior External Communications Manager at Alaska Airlines, noted.

“Through Atmos Rewards, we want to make the journey more rewarding and connect our members with the experiences they love, including making it easier to turn the day they arrive into part of the adventure,” she continued.

Travelers can find the latest participating resorts and offers on Alaska Airlines’ website.

For the 2026–’27 winter season, travelers flying into Jackson Hole Airport can receive a complimentary lift ticket at one of three nearby ski resorts, regardless of which airline they choose: Jackson Hole Mountain Resort, Snow King Mountain, or Grand Targhee Resort.

Each resort offers something slightly different. Snow King Mountain provides a full-day lift ticket, while Jackson Hole Mountain Resort and Grand Targhee offer half-day tickets. Snow King also offers night skiing on select evenings, giving travelers who arrive later in the day another opportunity to get on the mountain.

To redeem the offer, visitors must present their boarding pass or flight confirmation showing their arrival at Jackson Hole Airport, along with a matching photo ID, at the participating resort’s ticket window.

The complimentary ticket is only valid on the day of arrival, and blackout dates vary by resort.

For the 2026–’27 winter season, guests who reserve at least five nights of lodging through Big White Direct Bookings qualify for one free lift ticket on their arrival day. The offer is available for both new and existing eligible reservations and doesn’t require flying with a particular airline. To receive the complimentary ticket, guests must present their boarding pass.

Big White is about a 50-minute drive from Kelowna International Airport, and there is airport shuttle transportation available for those who prefer avoiding driving in the snow. For travelers arriving later in the afternoon, the resort also offers night skiing, allowing them to make use of their free ticket after dark.

Free arrival-day skiing isn’t limited to North America. In Chile, Ski Portillo offers guests the opportunity to ski on both their arrival and departure days as part of its all-inclusive vacation packages.

Located in the Andes Mountains beside Laguna del Inca, Ski Portillo operates during the Southern Hemisphere’s winter season, typically from June through September.

Unlike programs that require travelers to present an airline boarding pass, Ski Portillo includes arrival and departure day skiing in its seven-night packages and three- or four-night Mini Week stays.

Before booking, be mindful of your arrival time. Between collecting luggage, picking up rental equipment, and traveling from the airport to the resort, you may have less time on the mountain than expected. Booking an early flight can help maximize your ski day, while resorts offering night skiing may be better options for travelers arriving later.

It’s also important to check blackout dates and other restrictions, as some offers are only available during certain periods of the ski season. Additionally, some resorts may require reservations or specific booking arrangements to qualify for complimentary tickets.

Finally, don’t forget to keep your boarding pass. Many of these programs require proof of same-day air travel, and having everything ready when you arrive can help you get on the slopes that much faster.

#8203. How I Sent ‘The Prophet’ and ‘Free Rider’ on El Cap in 18.5 Hours

Left to right: Alex Honnold, Connor Herson, and Tommy Caldwell take a celebratory selfie at the top of 'The Prophet' on El Cap. (Photo: Courtesy of Alex Honnold)

My alarm goes off, but I’m already wide awake; I never sleep well before an early start. I’ve got half an hour to pull myself together before Alex gets here and we start hiking. As I choke down breakfast, I can’t help but wonder if I’m in over my head. Despite Alex and Tommy’s best reassurances, The Prophet scares me.

Established by Leo Houlding and Jason Pickles over a 10-year saga, The Prophet (5.13d/5.14a R; 1,800ft) has developed a reputation as one of El Cap’s scariest and most dangerous free routes. Indeed, it’s broken a few bones over the years, and to this day, Leo and Jason’s ground up attempt remains one of the boldest and most heroic chapters in El Cap’s history. Growing up, I always told myself that I’d never climb The Prophet. Maybe I’d rap into the A1 Beauty (the splitter crux pitch, rated 5.13d, though Leo, Sonnie Trotter, and Alex have all talked of upgrading it to 5.14a1) to try it, but the rest of the route was too dangerous for me—I don’t do dangerous stuff.

I wasn’t particularly surprised when Alex Honnold and Tommy Caldwell started trying The Prophet this season, but I watched their progress as a friend and spectator, not a potential suitor for the route. My own project on Leaning Tower was taking all my time this season.

On November 11, while eating breakfast and preparing for a day on my project, I ran into Alex and congratulated him on his send. He was hiking up that afternoon to belay Tommy, who was four days into his send push and trying the A1 Beauty. Alex offered to jumar and belay me on a ground-up push the next day, promising that the route was safer with his beta. I joked that I’d take him up if I couldn’t find a partner the next day for my project.

I had a very promising session on my project, but that afternoon, I was still partnerless for the following day, so I called up Alex to ask if his offer was still valid. In between Tommy’s redpoint goes on the A1, Alex called me back to tell me what gear I’d need. We planned to start climbing around 4:00 a.m. the following morning.

Packing up that evening, I felt wholly unprepared. I’d been sport climbing all summer and hadn’t done more than about six pitches in a day since spring. The only valley granite I’d touched this season was my overhanging, physical project on Leaning Tower, which was almost certainly a different style from the slabby, polished, and technical El Cap granite ahead of me. I’d need to re-adapt efficiently and quickly, working with a lower stamina threshold than I was used to.

Hiking up the following morning on November 12, Alex started breaking down the route for me. He told me how he and Tommy had cleaned all the pitches, how they ticked and recorded every gear placement. As I started leading the first few pitches, I realized just how helpful this was going to be: I took only the exact rack I’d need for each pitch, and I didn’t have to stress at all about beta or gear. I took Alex at his word about the relative safety of each section (a risky decision, I know…) and tried to turn my brain off to the fullest extent possible.

I settled into a sort of flow state; with the darkness obscuring any large runouts and Alex reassuring me of each gear placement ahead of me, I climbed calmly and intentionally over the lower pitches of the route. I couldn’t fathom Leo and Jason coming up here to find loose rock, grass-filled cracks, and no obvious route. It was certainly a far cry from my own experience on the freshly cleaned and ticked route. I remained relatively calm even over pitches four through six, the first few 5.13 pitches.

As we climbed higher and dawn broke, we saw Tommy above us; he’d not quite sent the night before, but he’d decided to spend another night on the wall and watch my attempt in the morning. With Tommy’s encouragement, I climbed the Guillotine Pitch (pitch eight, 5.13b), then the Devil’s Reacharound (pitch nine, 5.13a). Before long, I joined him at his portaledge at the base of the A1 Beauty just as the morning sun hit. What a perfect splitter it looked like, too—everything I could ever want in a pitch, at the very top of El Cap.

The A1 Beauty sees direct sun from first light until sunset, and it bakes. It was already quite warm, and I figured it would only get warmer as the day progressed. Without much waiting, I racked up and started what I thought would be a beta sussing mission. A few moves in, I realized this attempt could be more than just that; with Tommy hanging on a static rope above me, telling me exactly what to do, I found myself through the low crux (~V8), then through the next section. As I got higher and higher, I tried to push down the feeling that I might just pull it off on this first attempt and instead focus on each move, each foothold, each gear placement. It felt perfect. Before I knew it, I was at the next anchor, absolutely thrilled.

As excited as I was about the A1, suddenly the route became much more intense. I was only two pitches below the summit. Two pitches from flashing the entire route in a day. Two pitches from an El Cap flash. The following pitch was easy enough, but the exit pitch intimidated me: a 13b boulder problem right off the belay, involving an insecure standup on poor footholds.

I climbed up to the boulder and back down to the belay a few times, feeling increasingly nervous. Eventually, I went for it: I placed the foot, took a deep breath, and stood. The foot held, and I excitedly reached for the next hold, which guards easier climbing to the top. I briefly lost focus, allowing a small voice to say, I’m doing it! It’s happening! The next thing I knew, my foot had slipped and I was hanging on the rope. My flash go was botched.

At that moment, I lost all perspective of the incredible morning of climbing I’d had; I was devastated. Half an hour later, topping out The Prophet after successfully climbing the pitch, I felt the most hollow I’ve felt upon topping out El Cap. Alex and Tommy joined me on top. As they packed their haulbag and portaledge, I couldn’t help but regret my missed opportunity.

Within a few minutes, however, I regained some perspective. It had been an incredibly memorable morning of climbing, and I’d still freed The Prophet ground-up in about seven hours. Only that morning, doing this would have been a dream come true, and I smiled a bit. I checked the time: 11:30 a.m. “Wow! I can drive home and meet my family in time for dinner!” I laughed and joked to Tommy and Alex.

Alex turned and gave me a wry smile. “You know, you could do a Double right now. Compared to The Prophet, Free Rider will probably feel pretty easy.”

Tommy pitched in: “Yeah, I’d jug Free Rider this afternoon if you want!”

I stopped sorting my gear and stared. Great. I’m getting peer pressured by my heroes.

Among the rules I live by is that if Alex or Tommy offers something, I don’t turn them down. Especially a support mission on El Cap. As tired and emotionally drained as I was, I reminded myself just how much I’ve wanted to do the El Cap Double my entire life. I remembered topping out the free Nose-in-a-day last year, when I called every climber in the Valley to see if I could find a partner for a Double that day, to no avail. This sort of opportunity doesn’t come around particularly often. Even as I waffled about whether to go for it, the decision had been made. In a few hours’ time, I knew I’d be starting up Freeblast.

The climbing on Free Rider is significantly easier than on The Prophet, and I’d done most of the pitches when I freed the Salathé in 2022. I knew there would be little suspense about whether I’d be physically capable of sending it. However, I also knew I wasn’t in big walling shape, and besides, this would be far and away the most pitches I’ve climbed in a day. I remember watching the video of Tommy freeing the El Cap double back in 2005, where he nearly lost it at the Enduro Corner. I wondered if I was in for a similar bout.

The first few pitches on Free Rider went remarkably smoothly. Alex, still keen on supporting me, had jugged our day pack up the Heart Lines, which made Freeblast an absolute breeze. My feet were hurting, but I could feel the ibuprofen I’d pounded at the base starting to kick in. I settled into a flow, and pitch after pitch flew past. I felt remarkably fresh. With Tommy’s encouragement and psych, I was optimistic.

Around the Monster Offwidth (pitch 20 of 30 on Free Rider), darkness fell. I could feel the fatigue building; our pace slowed, but we kept moving. I was making a conscious effort to stay positive and cheerful, to act like I had endless energy in the hopes that I could fake that energy into existence.

When we reached the crux, I opted for the Teflon Corner instead of the Boulder Problem. I’d never tried the Boulder before, and I didn’t want my first attempt to be 40-odd pitches into the day. The Teflon went down on my first try, and before long, we were at the Enduro Corner. Tommy suggested that I skip the hanging belay at the end of the Enduro Corner and link it into the Round Table Traverse. I rolled my eyes, thinking that I’d be lucky to scrape my way up the Corner on its own, but to my surprise, I felt remarkably fresh. I reached the hanging belay and kept climbing, thankful to have cleared that last hurdle.

At 10:45 p.m., a little more than eight hours after starting Free Rider and 18.5 hours after starting up The Prophet, Tommy and I topped out to strong, cold winds. We didn’t stick around long to celebrate; already shivering, we quickly packed and started running to stay warm on the hike down. As we got lower and warmed up, however, we slowed down and soaked in the unforgettable day we’d just had: around 45 pitches of climbing for a free El Cap Double!

Alex and Tommy both have families. They both had good reason to rush home ahead of the incoming storm instead of supporting some kid who wanted to try their project. And to be honest, I wouldn’t have blamed them if they didn’t want me to mooch off their hard work prepping The Prophet. There’s absolutely no way I could have done The Prophet ground up and in a day without the labor Tommy and Alex spent to find the route, clean loose rock, and find all the gear beta. After four days on the wall and away from his family, I would have completely understood if Tommy wanted to get home to his kids rather than go up El Cap a second time that day—especially with Tioga Pass imminently closing, which meant supporting me on Free Rider would lengthen his drive home by about an hour.

Nevertheless, their support that day exemplifies the exact values I love to see in climbing. This is the sport I want climbing to be: one where the giants, the biggest legends of the game, are generous enough to go out of their way to help younger up-and-comers. A sport where the younger generation is not seen as a fresh wave of competition but is instead embraced and mentored.

Not flashing The Prophet is certainly going to sting for a while. I still replay that moment on the exit pitch daily, and I’m sure I’ll always feel some regret about it. Still, the more I reflect on that day, the more Alex and Tommy’s support stands out to me. Every outing leaves us with a lesson or slightly shifted worldview. In 10 or 20 years, I’m confident that looking back on the El Cap Double will remind me that there is a world larger than my own climbing; that, like Tommy and Alex, I can make another climber’s entire season by simply offering them a few hours of my time and a bit of encouragement. As I grow and find my place in the climbing world, I can only hope to be as influential a mentor to future generations.

1It’s hard to guess after only one attempt, but I wouldn’t argue with 5.14a for that pitch! I also could see upper-end 5.13d, though.

#8201. Mandatory Race Gear You’ll Actually Want to Use

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Many ultramarathons, including Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc (UTMB) require runners to carry certain gear. Cade Michael spent years as an unsponsored elite trail runner honing in his mandatory race kit with items that he both genuinely enjoys using and can be found affordably. He did this by taking advantage of sales, buying second-hand, and borrowing from friends. Here he shares his tips for building out your own race kit, including his favorite items in his pack.

Mandatory trail running race equipment is a lot like American health insurance: We all hate it. We’re all tempted to skimp on it. And we all inevitably need it when we’re least prepared. Required gear (or most of it, anyway) doesn’t have to be a waste of money or space. After spending yeas as an unsponsored runner curating my mandatory race gear, here’s my guide to getting gear that you’ll actually want to use more than once every 365 days, including my favorite items in my pack.

UTMB, among other races, often has extensive gear requirements and—whether you like to admit it or not—it’s usually for good reason. Weather and conditions can change rapidly in the mountains, and when you’re pushing your body to the extreme for hours (if not days) on end, as a general rule of thumb, it’s better to have it and not need it than to need it and not have it—particularly for race organizers’ liability insurance.

For example, while it may feel ridiculous for a 100K on the notoriously hot Western States 100 course in Auburn, California to make you carry a rain jacket and emergency blanket, the 2025 Canyons 100K  (on the same trails) saw snow at the start and highs around 40 degrees Fahrenheit. Packing three layers, two pairs of pants, and multiple pairs of gloves might seem like overkill for a day spent backcountry skiing in February, much less a running race in late August, but at the 2025 UTMB, ultrarunning’s most iconic race turned into a game of surviving the winter storm-like conditions.

I know all too well the allure of going light. But much like Admiral Ackbar’s epiphany at the Battle of Endor, it’s (usually) a trap. At the 2026 Twisted Fork Trail Festival in Park City, Utah, weather forecasts changed drastically in the 48 hours leading into race day, projecting relentless freezing rain. I chucked on a pair of gloves and arm sleeves and figured I’d warm up plenty as the race went on. As soon as we hit the first descent I lost feeling in my hands, feet, legs, cheeks, and plenty of other places I won’t call by name. My heart rate plummeted and I struggled for the entire remainder of the day. Eventual women’s champion, Rachel Drake, on the other hand, donned a warm base layer, long tights, gloves, and vest loaded with extras. Drake is an MD/PhD, mom, and professional runner for Nike ACG. Be more like Rachel, and less like me.

But you don’t have to hate the gear you’re going to buy one way or another to participate in these events.

Quality, packable gear can not only serve to save your race should conditions take a turn through the night in the Alps, but it can also save your run or, heaven forbid, life, if you’re spending any time out on the trails. While you could probably get away with using children’s XXS sized Walmart rain pants, your niece’s tiny pinky swim goggles, and Amazon’s finest two dollar headlamp, you can also use the mandatory equipment list of your next ultra as an excuse to get quality gear that won’t sit at the bottom of your junk drawer until next summer.

Here are my tips and tricks for getting good, lasting gear that’s a little easier on your bank account than the race entry fees and international travel.

Required kit, in most cases, isn’t going to be the product you wear holes through everyday. One is built to be versatile, lightweight, and packable while the other is made for a specific purpose and durability. Some pieces of equipment, like your rain coat for UTMB, are ones you want to stand up in the most brutal of conditions. Others, like a secondary headlamp, are areas you might be able to save some weight and cash.

Lightweight, packable gear is usually updated every year just like the rest of a brand’s product line and often goes on sale during off-season months or discount days (ahem, Black Friday or REI member days). A lot of years, the only update is the colorway, so just get the highlighter yellow and own it!

Better yet, buy gear second hand. Many of the products I’ll list below I grabbed from resale sites like Poshmark or Mercari for a fraction of the retail price

It may seem obvious, but always get your size. It might seem worth it to save a few grams and get a women’s XXS when you’re in the Chamonix Arc’teryx store panic-buying a rain jacket 24 hours before the gun goes off, but I promise you it’s not. Get the extra ounce and future you will be proud of the responsible decision to get something you’ll actually put on your body.

If you’re questioning whether a piece of gear will satisfy the requirements set by race organizers for your next ultra, err on the side of caution. Get the marginal gains wherever you can within reason, but I promise you trimming two centimeters off your bandaging or emergency blanket will not make Col du Grand Ferret any easier or quicker.

People in your run club and or training partners have probably raced an ultra and used this stuff before. If it’s not something you will need time and time again, it’s OK to borrow it; chances are, they won’t need it in the next week or two anyway. The more you share, the more you save.

Get familiar with your equipment. Try it in training, just like you would a pair of shoes or a nutrition product. Being able to mindlessly locate and use your gear will pay dividends when you have no mindfulness left late into an ultra. Brand-spanking-new isn’t always best.

If you’re between two rain jackets, just get the one with the extra zipper. The best gear is the gear you use. Ruth Croft and Tom Evans won a historically cold and wet UTMB in 2026. When they bundled up through the night, I’m certain they were rocking the clothes they trusted to get the job done, not the ones that came in a few grams under. You’re racing an ultra marathon through the mountains, not a 5K parkrun.

Please keep reading, my opinions are important. Seriously though, whether it’s one of our gear roundups (shameless plug) or your favorite YouTuber, people put dozens of pieces through countless miles so you don’t have to. Take a few extra minutes to read a few pros and cons before you pull the trigger.

A lot of thought and stress can go into mandatory equipment, but don’t let it take away from the race experience. At my first UTMB race, UTMB Whistler in Canada, the cold-weather gear policy was implemented two days before the race due to a snowstorm. I’d just come from racing in California and Spain in September, so I didn’t have a suitcase stocked with skimpy mandatory equipment. Luckily for me, I couldn’t afford to grab a bunch of last-second gear and just used what I had with me. Retrospectively, my pack was a little heavier and bulkier than it could have been had I been properly prepared, but I didn’t think about the weight once during the race. But boy, was I glad to have warm gloves and a beanie that fit.

Here’s a list of some of my favorite mandatory equipment I’ve amassed over a couple of years of racing in Chamonix as an unsponsored athlete.

This one is totally optional and, frankly, probably only applicable for a shorter ultra like MCC or OCC during UTMB week. The mini phone is a great tool to have if you’re only out for a handful of hours. So long as you ensure you get a SIM card that has roaming and data enabled for whatever country or region you will be running through, it can call, text, Whatsapp, and even Strava. UTMB requires you to have a smart phone capable of downloading and using the LiveTrail app, and this Google Play Store enabled pocket rocket is the smallest you can get while satisfying the requirements. It also takes pretty cool retro camcorder-style videos. For the longer races like CCC and UTMB, however, it’s probably your safest bet to just bring along your standard, daily driver smart phone. You have to keep your phone on at all times throughout the race, and the number of charging bricks you’d have to haul to keep this thing running through the night outsizes any weight savings it might provide.

Typically, flasks are flasks. Your running vest will usually come with a couple that fit. That being said, I usually hate running vests. One of the primary reasons is the way traditional flasks sit in the sleeves, bouncing around and uncomfortably rubbing against my collarbone. My pro tip here is to check out flasks with smaller lids like these Hydrapak pocket flasks. Theoretically, they’re made to fit flush with your running belt, but I’ve found they are less bulky and front heavy in a running vest, too. (As long as they fit in the sleeves.)

A sure bet to be on the required kit list for almost any ultra is a waterproof rain jacket. UTMB’s specifications are rather persnickety, with required minimum waterproof rating, breathability score, sealed seams, and an integrated hood. The On Ultra Jacket lives up to demands while remaining paper thin, uber light, and incredibly packable. It can end up feeling a little too trash-baggy and unbreathable to be your workhorse running jacket, but nevertheless it’s a great piece to be able to throw in your pack anytime you head up into the unpredictable weather of the alpine.

For headlamps, I always keep a couple of options hanging around for the varying amount of daylight in different races. For OCC, for example, I opt for the Petzl E+Lite. It’s so small and light it’s an almost imperceptible item to carry and it uses nickel-sized 2432 batteries, but, as you might expect, that means it is useless for anything more than an hour or so in a pinch.

For longer races where you will inevitably be running through hours of darkness, if not the entire night, this is not somewhere to skimp on weight. A popular option in this category is the Petzl Iko Core, which features an incredible 500 lumen bulb, outstanding shine time, and a replaceable battery that sits at the back of the crown for stability. If you’re running UTMB, don’t forget to pick up the mandatory red light filter for fragile wildlife areas.

The crown jewel of mandatory equipment is the running vest. It’s what will hold all of your other mandatory equipment. It’s what will be in direct contact with your body and can make or break the convenience and comfortability of your racing experience. But, most importantly, it’s what will show up in all your post-race photos and make you look either super nerdy or really cool—by which I mean slightly less nerdy. In all seriousness, choosing your hydration vest is critical—and critically personal. Salomon and Nathan offer popular options that have dominated the category dating back to the cradle of civilization. (Hammurabi allegedly kept his chisel in an ADVskin 5L.) But the market is flooding with alternatives as the sport continues to grow, so there is no shortage of options. The most important things to consider are fit and layout. For my preferences, which is for my vest to feel as least like a vest as possible, the Tantrums Crest 6 and Kiprun Pro Team 5L have been excellent. The pocket layouts have tons of nooks and crannies that scratch my obnoxious need for hyperorganization better than keeping foods from touching on my Thanksgiving plate. They have minimal bounce, soft fabric across the shoulder straps, and offer a rear tunnel pocket for an extra flask. Both the Tantrums and Kiprun also come in light colors, a touch that seems a blatant choice for any piece of athletic equipment but was, until recently, a white whale on the hydration vest market.

A good cap is indispensable and obviously extends beyond race day. It’s not that deep, just get one that feels and looks good. Ciele is a sure fire way to fit in at the coolest run club in town.

Waterproof pants can be a tricky one. They’re probably the thing you’ll use the least in everyday training (save for the tinfoil-esque emergency blanket), and they’re one of the most expensive pieces of kit on the list. Getting a pair that satisfies UTMB’s specifications and doesn’t necessitate a 25-liter pack to fit is going to be steep. On makes the Ultra Pant compliment to the aforementioned jacket, but I use these Rab Phantom Pants. The two are kind of “six-one, half-dozen another,” so just grab whichever you can find on a last-season sale.

#8200. How My First Multi-Pitch Climb Became a Midnight Barefoot Epic

On July 4, 2026, Audrey Callaway climbed her first real multi-pitch: Diedre (5.8, 6 pitches) in Squamish, B.C. The catch? She didn’t start up pitch one until nearly 9 p.m., thus becoming voluntarily benighted in only the most literal sense of the term. “My story isn’t a disaster!” Callaway explains. “It’s about learning, the tenacity of a little psych, and extremely good company.”

After first getting into the sport at a gym in Chicago, Callaway later moved to upstate New York near the Gunks. Currently, she’s studying forestry at the University of Vermont. “I like trees, I like climbing, I like birds,” she says of her big three hobbies. She’s mostly a boulderer and sport climber who wants to get more into trad climbing. She also works at a climbing gym.

Callaway wanted to share her experience to highlight the growing pains of “doing things poorly the first time”—and how the right partners ease those pains. Below, she shares her story and what others embarking on their first multi-pitch can learn from her experience.

It’s really cool to feel very bad at something again.

I was planning to visit my girlfriend Lucy, who had been in Squamish for the whole summer. Then my best friend Will, who I grew up climbing with at the gym, told me he also happened to be going out to Squamish. I got there a few days before him and did a little bouldering.

When Will got there, he was even more psyched than I was. After bouldering all afternoon, we’re sitting around, playing chess and looking through Lucy’s guidebook when we saw a trad climb that looked so cool: Diedre (5.8, 6 pitches).

It was 7 p.m., but the sun didn’t set until around 9 p.m. It was very spur of the moment. We’re just like, “We gotta do this thing.” So we quickly got all our stuff together.

We knew it was going to get dark. It’s not like it snuck up on us. But Lucy had a lot of experience. Will and I didn’t know how to trad climb at this point, although he learned later on that trip. So she’s carrying the team. Afterward, she told me she brought only a single rack so that she could share in our sense of adventure and “empathize with the uncertainty.”

First, we got super lost on the way there. We didn’t get to the base of the climb until like 8:45 p.m., but it was still super bright out.

Very quickly, I realized how bad I was at rope management. I was in the middle, belaying Lucy, and we had two ropes. Routefinding is something that you take for granted when you’ve been climbing outside for a while. I was taking the path of most resistance. There was a pretty solid crack on really good terrain, but I’m newer to crack climbing, so I was not about to put my hands in there and trust that. Instead, I was doing this very sketchy 5.10 slab. Eventually, I started using the crack.

We got up to the first belay and we’re all on top of each other because we don’t really know where to be. Nothing was unsafe, but it was very slow. Lucy started going up this 5.6 very runout slab. But I had looped a knot of rope around where I was belaying. I didn’t realize that until I’d fed out enough of the slack. So I kept shorting her like every five feet. I knew that there was totally a way to fix this, but I don’t know how.

Then the sun set. That’s okay, because we had headlamps—but Lucy’s headlamp was dead. It was funny because before we started climbing, Lucy was like, “Guys, make sure you have your headlamps.” But then when we put them on, she’s like, “Can I actually borrow yours?”

So she took mine, and now I was climbing in the dark on slab. It was very precarious, but beautiful. It felt so scary in the moment. But the town was right there, we’re on the most classic 5.8 ever, and we’re a hundred feet off the ground—it wasn’t actually that scary.

Will and I both had super competitive shoes on. It had been two hours at this point and we’re standing on this slab and our feet were killing us. Every time I left the belay, Will told me he “would lowkey start crying a bit” because he knew he’d have to climb soon, enduring more toe pain. So we both took off our shoes because it’s easier to climb barefoot. Now I was barefoot in the dark on this slab.

Every time we got to a new belay, we tried to make the system better. Lucy was just trying to climb, but we’re shorting her every time. Now Will was in the way. We were right on top of each other.

None of these things were particularly hard challenges. If we knew what we were doing, we could have fixed any one of these problems in 30 seconds. I would get back up to Lucy and she would be like, “Why didn’t you just do this?” Then something else would come up.

At one point, probably around 11:30 p.m., Will got a cam stuck. Lucy’s like, “Try wiggling it.” She told him to pull upward, but he said it was literally impossible. Lucy lowered down and pulled it out, first try. There must have been times like this when Lucy was frustrated, but she never showed it. Will describes Lucy as the most patient person he’s ever met.

We got to the top at midnight. It was hypnotizing on the apron. The lights of town beneath us glowed surreally. I smoked my first cigarette at the top.

I remember walking back and it was really quiet. We got back on the road and our gear’s rattling and the moon’s out. It was so quiet and peaceful.

It was one in the morning when we got back to the campground by the Chief. We didn’t want to be disrespectful with a big light, so we put a headlamp under this pickle jar we had. By the light of this pickle lamp, we ate pickles and cold canned minestrone and asked, “What are we gonna do tomorrow?”

To really be benighted, I would say it has to sneak up on you. It kinda felt like it snuck up on me. Clearly, as a group we were aware it was about to happen. But I was surprised when all of a sudden it was dark and I had no headlamp and was climbing barefoot. It made me feel like a salamander, really in touch with the rock.

Lucy and I did another multi-pitch the next day, and since then I’ve done a couple two-pitch climbs in the Gunks when I got back to New York. I will probably do lots of really awesome multi-pitches in my lifetime that are beautiful and scenic with really hard climbing, but I’m never gonna have another one that bad. I’m never gonna have another first one.

As told to Maya Silver. This story has been edited for length, structure, and clarity.

#8199. The Tour du Mont Blanc Is Getting New Rules in 2027. Having a Guide Is More Important Than Ever.

A view of the of the Alps on Tour du Mont Blanc. (Photo: Getty)

The trail ahead of us narrows to a ledge, with rock on our left and a sheer drop on our right, camouflaged by trees. After hearing the now-familiar heavy breaths of runners behind me, I move to the mountainside to let them pass. It’s mid-August, and the Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc (UTMB), the ultramarathon circling Mont Blanc, is kicking off later this month in Chamonix. We started our own Tour du Mont Blanc in Chamonix, the mountain town known as the birthplace of alpinism, which was buzzing with excitement and packs of runners strapped into hydration packs. Ahead of me, a young man is stopped on the narrow dirt trail, calling out to a friend on the forest slope below. Before I can even turn around, our guide, Jason Day, springs into action, grabs a rope from his pack, and helps pull the hiker, whose pack had tumbled down the slope, back to safety.

Moments like that are becoming more common with more trekkers on the Tour du Mont Blanc (TMB), the 170-kilometer (106-mile) loop around Western Europe’s highest peak through France, Italy, and Switzerland. Roughly 80,000 people hike it each year, and visits are up about 50 percent since 2020. “People can only see the backsides of those in front of them,” Jean-Marc Peillex, mayor of Saint-Gervais-les-Bains, a mountain town at the base of Mont Blanc in France, told Swiss broadcaster SRF. That wasn’t my exact experience for most of the trek, but in a few places, especially near Chamonix, the trail was congested.

Chamonix and the six other French towns along the TMB route, from Vallorcine to Bourg-Saint-Maurice and Beaufort, have drafted a charter to manage crowds, with local officials aiming to put it in place by spring 2027, ahead of next year’s trekking season. The new rules, aiming to curb overtourism and help slow environmental damage, are awaiting final signature. The key proposals include reservations for every night on the trail; a ban on wild camping, with paid, bookable bivouac areas replacing the informal spots; and new limits on luggage transfers. Guided groups would be capped at twelve and led by guides trained in rescue and licensed in all three countries.

The charter is voluntary, covers only France for now, and still depends on local ordinances for enforcement. But the message is clear: the era of showing up and figuring it out on the TMB is ending. Chamonix’s mayor, François-Xavier Laffin, who is similarly introducing quotas at nearby Lac Blanc, an alpine lake also suffering from its popularity, puts it this way: “To reserve is to preserve.”

Adding to the growing traffic on the trail are the effects of climate change on the Alps. Rising summer temperatures are accelerating permafrost thaw and glacier retreat, contributing to record rockfall activity in the Mont Blanc massif. While this mostly impacts the summit climbing routes, hot summers also change trail and water conditions for hikers on the Tour du Mont Blanc.

“As for the environmental impacts, trail erosion is of course the most obvious one, but we must also take into account wild bivouacking, which has multiplied, with impacts on the flora as well as the disturbance of wildlife,” says Daniel Rodrigues, general director of the Compagnie des Guides de Chamonix, the oldest mountain guide organization in the world.

“The reservation system is fair. Everyone can book their places, and tour operators can do the same. So the same rules apply to everyone, including amateur mountain users, and that matters to us: the mountains are a space of freedom,” says Rodrigues. “That said, this space must be protected, in terms of biodiversity and environmental impacts, but also economically.”

The charter puts licensed mountain professionals at the center of safety on the trail. According to Rodrigues, that means operators will no longer be able to sell self-guided packages (just bookings and transfers) and will have to include a guide certified in all three countries.

“This is a major step forward, because the guide ensures that everyone stays safe and that everything goes smoothly. It also creates work for local people and delivers a genuine positive impact on the inhabitants of this mountain range,” adds Rodrigues.

I hiked the Tour du Mont Blanc in August with Live Breathe Hike, and I came home convinced that, especially under the potential new rules, having a local guide is no longer a luxury. It’s the smartest way to hike this trail.

The TMB isn’t one trail; rather, there are a lot of different paths and detours.”There’s a classic route, but there’s a lot of different variants,” says Allison Fleece, cofounder of WHOA Travel, a women’s adventure-travel company that runs guided trips, including on the Tour du Mont Blanc. Some variants are higher and more exposed; others go along lower valleys. On our third day, instead of following the crowds, Day led us off the Col du Bonhomme on a variant toward Lac de Roselend, where we barely saw another hiker for miles. “You feel like you have the place to yourself,” says Live Breathe Hike founder Tanya Perret, who started the Chamonix-based trekking company in 2016 and says she has guided the TMB more than 75 times.

Under the proposed rules, every night would have to be booked in advance, across three countries with different systems. Guides already do that work, and finding gems to stay at like Le Chalet de Roselend takes deep knowledge of the area. With only ten rooms, the chalet, whose balconies overlook the Lac de Roselend, was a godsend after one of our longest days of trekking. Years ago, Perret drove there to book it in person, because the elderly owner at the time only took reservations face to face. The young couple who now runs it cooks traditional dishes with local produce.

The charter asks operators to buy local and partner with local producers. Good guides already do. “Many of the places that we stay are generational families, and I’ve known those families for 30 years,” says Perret. On our trip, that meant a stop at a family cheese farm as well as the small lakeside chalet. “That’s the micro-economy,” adds Perret.

Nearly every day on my trek, Day chose a variant. Perret says the choice comes down to two factors: where accommodation is available and which trail will give the group the best experience that day.

The variants usually turned out to be my favorite stretches. Self-guided trekkers can research the variants, but a guide knows which one fits the day. “By giving your guides a little bit of autonomy, it means they can just tweak things here and there, which makes for a unique journey,” says Perret.

“The weather patterns change a lot in the mountains and they change really fast,” adds Fleece, who partners with Compagnie des Guides de Chamonix on their guided TMB trips. “Guides have years and years, most of the time decades, of experience.” A guide, she says, can help you avoid dicey situations, “but also, if you get yourself into a dicey situation, having a guide is like a safety measure to get you quickly and swiftly out of it.”

Day has been trekking Tour Du Mont Blanc since 1992 and knows the ever-changing mountain conditions demand quick judgment. On a recent trip up Mont Blanc’s Italian route, he and his climbing partner turned back in poor snow. “We binned the whole trip,” he says. Two friends kept going, and on a ridge with snow cornices on both sides, one side broke away. “Either side could have gone,” he says.

Multi-day treks around the world are my favorite way to travel. With WHOA, I’ve summited Kilimanjaro and Mount Elbrus, Europe’s tallest peak (not Mont Blanc, as many assume). I’ve taken guided trips on the Trans Bhutan Trail and Japan’s Shikoku pilgrimage, which were not nearly as challenging but would have been far less rich experiences without learning the culture from our local guides. I’ve trekked the full O Trek in Patagonia without a guide, but with friends and the help of the company Chile Nativo for booking refuges. Half of the O circuit, the W Trek, I hiked alone. So I know the benefits of taking guided multi-day treks and hiking alone at your own pace, stopping when you want.

I can understand why travelers would want to do the TMB without a guide; many hikers do so without any issue. You can go at your own speed and take a long break for an afternoon coffee at a refuge with an open table facing the sun. A guided trip costs more. Middle options have been growing, including self-guided packages that handle the bookings for you, but even those require your due diligence and research, and could be affected by these new rules for 2027.

One day on the trek, we stopped for lunch at a refuge and ran into a woman with a bandaged hand. She and her friend were on a self-guided trip whose itinerary, she told us, had started them on their first day hiking one of the route’s most exposed stretches—the ladders below Tête aux Vents—where she got injured. On the standard counterclockwise route, that section usually comes at the very end. Day told us that those ladders can easily be bypassed in busy seasons or wet weather.

If you want to escape the crowds on the Tour du Mont Blanc, guides know the variants that lead to the quietest parts of the trail. Except for a few days, on certain passes, we managed to find stretches where it was just us, as far as I  could see. On our fourth day, we crossed the Col de la Seigne into Italy, past a block of granite barely knee-high: the real border marker, not the big monument nearby. I’d have walked right past it. My guide didn’t let me.

#8198. Stephanie Case Just Ran 100 Miles in Antarctica. She Doesn’t Even Like the Cold.

In 2025, a photo of Stephanie Case breastfeeding her infant daughter, Pepper, at an aid station during a 100K ultra in Northern Wales went viral, and the human rights lawyer and ultrarunner became the face of postpartum badassery.

Now, she’s officially the first woman to run 100 miles in Antarctica. Case took on the November 8 challenge in part to prove that the things she did before becoming a mom weren’t behind her. If anything, she could come back and do them even better.

“The whole idea for this race came after I had my daughter and people were asking me if I was going to start to settle down,” Case, 44, shared with Trail Runner from her home in Chamonix, France. “They were criticizing me after I came back for my first race postpartum, telling me that I was selfish to be taking that time to train. So I wanted to go out and really prove to myself and remind myself that I could keep doing big things.”

Actually, big is an understatement. Of the eight runners who started the Antarctic Ice Ultra 100 miler on Union Glacier, Case was one of four finishers, and second overall. Her finishing time of 17 hours, 31 minutes and 39 seconds, a clip of 10:31 per mile, smashed the former overall course record by five hours. Only Yusheng Ni, a top ultrarunner from China with experience racing in Antarctica, ran faster in a new best-ever mark of 17:02:24.

Here’s the kicker: Case doesn’t even like running in the cold.

There’s cold, and then there’s Antarctica cold. The race started at 1 a.m. under a 24-hour sun, with temperatures as low as minus 35 degrees Fahrenheit—roughly 35 degrees colder than a typical kitchen freezer. And with fierce polar winds, no exposed skin is safe.

“I’m someone who doesn’t like when the house goes below room temperature. My partner and I are constantly having a fight about where we set the thermostat,” Case shared. “So this was going to be a big challenge for me. I knew that I wasn’t going to love it. But I’m Canadian. There’s no bad weather, there’s just bad clothing, they say.”

Finding the right gear was one of the biggest priorities in Case’s preparation. She reached out to other runners who had completed the Antarctic 100-miler in previous years to glean their insight. One offered an unexpected tip: Apply sunscreen inside of her nostrils, since the sun reflecting off the snow can burn there, too.

She also worked with The North Face, one of her sponsors, to design a custom shoe specifically for the conditions. Breathability was key: She didn’t want moisture trapped inside the shoe, and the sole needed to remain flexible in extreme temperatures. There was also the matter of laces. Frozen laces—or having to tie them with mittens on—were not an option. The solution was a BOA closure system, which let her tighten the shoes by turning a dial. The design also included an integrated, insulated but breathable gaiter and removable spikes she could screw into the soles if conditions got icy.

The setup worked better than she could have hoped. Case wore two pairs of socks—a thin liner underneath a wool pair—and didn’t change them once during the entire race.

“I just set it and left it,” she said. “And it was one of the things I was most stressed about, because with hands, you can put on more gloves. You can have hand warmers. But toe warmers don’t work when you’re running. They can’t fit in the shoe. And I knew if my toes were cold, I was just going to be screwed. And they were toasty the whole time.”

As for the rest of her clothing, Case had to consider another challenge: her sweat rate.

“I’m a heavy sweater. Even in just mild cold temperatures, I sweat a liter an hour, and in warm temperatures up to two liters,” she said. “So I knew that I would be at a pretty big disadvantage, because when you sweat, your gear gets wet and then you’re screwed.”

Her strategy was to dress as lightly as possible through her core while keeping her hands, feet and face warm and protected. In the coldest stretches, she wore winter tights under wind pants, along with a thin base layer, a midlayer, and a shell on top. At some points, she stripped down to a thin base layer and shell.

“As long as I kept moving, I was fine,” she said. “But I wouldn’t be able to kind of stop and walk if something went wrong.”

She never quite felt warm, and some exposed skin on her face did get frostbitten. But she managed to find moments of equilibrium.

“I felt comfortable at times. And then other times I feel like I was just constantly on the edge,” she said. “I wasn’t freezing, but I was cold. But as long as my feet were OK and my hands were OK, then I was fine to keep moving.”

The temperature wasn’t the only feature of Antarctica that concerned Case. She describes herself as a “mountain goat.” Living in Chamonix, she’s accustomed to steep trails and vert—not the flat, repetitive terrain of Antarctica’s 38-loop course.

Working with her coach, Meghan Roche, she shifted her training toward flatter ground and faster running. The change paid off: during her workouts, Case set personal records at several distances, from the 10K through the marathon.

“I had a love-hate relationship with it,” she said of the training. “But the funny thing was that every time I had a training session, I was getting PRs, because I just don’t run on flat ground.”

She also tested her gear in a cryotherapy chamber during a trip to Geneva, Switzerland, spending 20 minutes in temperatures that gradually warmed from minus 148°F to minus 22°F. The goal wasn’t so much to acclimate as to understand what the cold would feel like and test her logistics. The session made her rethink her fueling plan: Pulling off gloves, unzipping a shell, and drinking from a flask in those conditions would be too cumbersome.

Instead, her camera operator doubled as her crew, handing her a SIS gel and flask every loop. While most competitors visited the aid tent every lap or two, Case aimed to go ten loops—roughly a marathon—between stops. She had to cut the first stretch short when her balaclava froze into a solid block of ice, but after that she managed three 10-loop stints.

The aid station offered some reprieve, with ramen noodles, mashed potatoes, shots of maple syrup, and Rice Krispies treats, but even small tasks there got complicated. Taking her gloves off for just 30 seconds to go to the bathroom could mean waiting 20 minutes for her hands to warm up again.

“There was not a single minute during this race when I kind of just relaxed and allowed myself to switch off,” she says. “In any other 100, I can usually just kind of push past [discomfort], but there, one tiny mistake could end the race for me.”

As Case recovers at home with collagen mask treatments to heal her frostbitten cheeks and nose, her next challenge is already on the calendar: becoming the first woman to complete the Montane Arctic Spine, a 500-kilometer race in February. This time, she’ll be on Nordic skis, pulling a sled and traveling solo, with checkpoints as far as 50 miles apart. She’ll need to melt her own snow, pitch her own tent, and carry out the journey without a crew.

She hopes Antarctica has prepared her for an even harder task.

“Sometimes the way to get through a really scary thing is to line up an even scarier thing afterwards,” she said.

Beyond that, Case is developing a project called “94 Degrees,” a film that will show her running the gamut of conditions from minus 40 degrees Celsius in the Arctic to 54 degrees Celsius at Badwater in California’s Death Valley, a 94-degree Celsius spread. (She’s qualified for Badwater but still needs to apply for an invitation, so that part isn’t yet confirmed.)

And in the meantime, she’ll continue her work for the U.N. while serving as the President of Free to Run, a non-profit organization that uses sport to empower women and girls in conflict-affected areas. And she’ll soak up all the cuddles she can with Pepper, now 2, while sharing stories of that one time she ran 100 miles in Antarctica. It’s a story that almost sounds like a fairy tale.

“I actually brought one of her toys, a penguin rubber ducky, with me on the trip, just as a reminder of her,” Case said. “And then this penguin came out on the course and actually ran alongside me for part of it. I’ve been showing her photos and videos … but still … it’s all kind of unbelievable.”

#8197. A Hiker Died Along the PCT After Winter Ice Turned a Popular Trail Dangerous

Snow covers the slopes of Southern California's San Gabriel Mountains, where a hiker died on November 22 after reportedly slipping on ice and falling approximately 500 feet on Mount Baden-Powell (Photo: Noah Sauve/Getty Images)

A hiker died on November 22 after reportedly slipping on ice and falling approximately 500 feet while trying to help his son on Mount Baden-Powell, a 9,399-foot peak in Southern California’s San Gabriel Mountains, according to a GoFundMe organized by the hiker’s niece.

The GoFundMe page identified the man as Guillermo Alejandro Batres. His niece, Jennifer Morse, wrote on the fundraising page that Batres and his son were attempting to summit the mountain when the younger man slipped and fell. When Batres tried to help him up, he lost his footing and fell down a steep gulch.

“On this mountain, there’s no room for error if you slip when it’s snowy or icy out,” Cris Hazzard, a Southern California hiking expert who has climbed Baden-Powell dozens of times, told Outside. “If you slip in the summer, you probably just fall on your butt, maybe go down some gravel. You slip in the winter, you’re going down hundreds, if not thousands, of feet.”

AV Scanner News, a local outlet that monitors emergency dispatches, reported that authorities received a call about the incident around 10:09 A.M. after the hikers encountered snow and ice roughly three miles from the Vincent Gap trailhead. Los Angeles County firefighters and sheriff’s deputies responded near mile marker 71 on Angeles Crest Highway. Authorities also requested the sheriff’s department’s Air Rescue 5 helicopter crew to recover Batres’s body, according to the outlet.

Authorities have not independently confirmed the family’s account of the fall, and the sheriff’s department did not respond to Outside‘s request for comment before publication.

Located in Angeles National Forest northeast of Los Angeles, Baden-Powell is a popular warm-weather climb. The standard summit route begins at Vincent Gap, a 6,585-foot mountain pass along Angeles Crest Highway. From there, hikers follow the Pacific Crest Trail for roughly four miles, climbing more than 2,800 feet through 35 wooded switchbacks up the mountain’s north face before reaching an exposed ridge near the summit.

Because the mountain’s north-facing slopes receive less direct sunlight, snow tends to linger there, Hazzard told Outside. During warmer days, that snow can melt and refreeze overnight, leaving patches of ice along the trail. Although the San Gabriel Mountains receive snow every winter, the conditions can catch visitors off guard so close to Los Angeles.

Batres had hiked Baden-Powell at least once before, according to the GoFundMe, and Hazzard noted that even experienced hikers face heightened risk once ice forms on the route.

“If you are experienced and you know the dangers, there’s still a higher risk of something going wrong than there would be without that snow or ice, regardless of how careful you are,” Hazzard said. “Each winter, we get people going up there who don’t really understand that the hike they did in the summer is now a mountaineering exercise. It’s so steep, and there are dangerous runouts. If you slip, you might hit your head. There’s a lot you can bang into on the way down.”

Batres’s death occurred just two days after another hiker survived a serious fall on the same mountain. In a November 21 statement on X, the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department described rescuing a hiker who had slid more than 300 feet down a snowy chute on Baden-Powell on November 20.

Responders initially struggled to locate the person due to inaccurate GPS coordinates, completing the rescue shortly before worsening weather would have grounded the helicopter.

Similar falls have occurred in past winters. In February 2016, a 69-year-old hiker slid roughly 100 feet down an icy chute before a sheriff’s helicopter airlifted him to a trauma center. Nearby Mount Baldy has also experienced deadly winter accidents, including three hiking fatalities in the first week of January 2026.

Despite having climbed Baden-Powell in winter with experienced mountaineers using crampons, Hazzard said he now avoids the peak once snow arrives. Instead, he recommends seeking formal mountaineering training before attempting snow-covered summits or choosing lower-elevation desert trails around Joshua Tree and Palm Springs.

“They shouldn’t do it in the winter,” Hazzard said. “But winter is the great time to go and do the hikes you can’t safely do in summer, and leave the high peaks alone.”
