#8182. Skiing Takes a Toll on Your Knees. Here’s the Muscle You Need to Strengthen, According to an Orthopedic Surgeon.

(Photo: Monster walk exercise: Erstudiostok/Getty; Design: Ayana Underwood/Canva)

Strong legs are essential for skiing without injury. But many traditional strength training programs focus on the bigger muscles in your lower half, including the quads, hamstrings, and gluteus maximus (your largest butt muscle).

That means the smaller guys often get neglected. And one small guy in particular, the gluteus medius, which forms part of your side butt, is worth paying attention to if you actually want to reduce your risk of knee pain and injury this winter.

Because ACL tears are among the most common ski injuries, Dr. Gregory Lichtman, an orthopedic surgeon in northern California and a physician for the U.S. women’s ski team, puts heavy emphasis on strengthening the glute medius. In his view, it’s one of the most important muscles for staying safe and skiing well.

Unfortunately, even high-level athletes can have a weak glute medius, according to Lichtman. That’s because unlike the quads, hamstrings, calves, and glute max—which can naturally get strong from activities like road running and hill climbing—the glute medius typically needs to be intentionally strengthened.

Read on to learn why this small muscle is so important, Lichtman’s favorite way to strengthen it, and other essential fitness tips for injury prevention.

The glute medius is a small muscle on your outer hip that fires up when you bring your leg out to the side, a motion known as hip abduction. It also helps control the knee by preventing it from caving inward (a position known as valgus) as you perform various movements. And it assists you in balancing on one leg, which is important when loading your downhill ski, Lichtman says.

In skiing, if you get into the back seat (meaning, you shift your body weight backward, instead of staying centered over your skis) and the knee goes into valgus, the tibia can internally rotate, “and that’s where the ACL tears occur,” Lichtman says. Even if you don’t get a full-blown ACL tear, going into valgus when you ski can contribute to patellofemoral pain syndrome, a fancy term for pain at the front of the kneecap, Lichtman says.

By strengthening the glute medius, you can make it more resistant to valgus in the first place, which decreases your chances of both ACL tears and general knee pain.

There are also performance benefits: “A strong gluteus medius also really allows you to stand on your downhill ski a little bit more aggressively and really make a more aggressive turn,” Lichtman says. That’s because when you place most of your weight on your downhill ski (the one that’s closest to the bottom of the hill), your G-forces will want to throw you down the mountain. But having a strong glute medius, in addition to strong quads and core muscles, helps form a strong pillar on your outer hip, which “really allows you to withstand those G-forces the best,” Lichtman says.

One of the classic ways to target the glute medius is to strap on ankle weights, lie on your side, and lift and lower your top leg. Lichtman says. This exercise can absolutely strengthen your glute medius, but it’s not Lichtman’s go-to. That’s because it primarily just isolates that muscle and doesn’t mimic how we move in sports.

A better bet, Lichtman says, is to focus on exercises that simultaneously activate the gluteus medius and other muscle groups because that better resembles how we use this muscle during athletics. His favorite exercise that ticks that box? The monster walk. Not only does this move really fire up the gluteus medius, but it also works the core, hamstrings, quads, and glute max, he says.

Incorporate this exercise into your workouts three days a week, with at least one day off between sessions so the muscle has the downtime it needs to recover and build back stronger. To stave off boredom and also work different parts of your hips and quads, incorporate different variations of the monster walk throughout the week. For example, instead of stepping straight out to the side, step forward and back, or diagonally forward and diagonally back. As long as you have good form and keep your legs spread apart so that you feel tension from the band the whole time, “all directions can be effective,” Lichtman says.

Lichtman suggests doing monster walks during both pre-season and throughout ski season. “One of the big pitfalls is that we will all get ready for ski season, and then taper off our dry land training,” he explains. “If you’re one of the fortunate few who can ski five or six days a week, you’re probably getting enough exercise, and you probably don’t want to stress your body out any more than that. But for those of us who are skiing two to three days a week, finding some time to do some cross-training and continue to work on our core and our hip abductor strength is really important because those are the less commonly used muscles during skiing.”

Once this exercise becomes easy, level up the challenge by using a stronger resistance band.

A strong glute medius can keep you safe on the slopes. But it’s not the only fitness-related aspect of injury prevention.

A strong core and quads, along with good overall endurance, are also key. That’s because one of the essential components of an ACL tear pattern in skiing is getting kicked into the back seat. And while the gluteus medius helps guard against knee valgus in this position, it doesn’t prevent you from getting into the back seat in the first place, Lichtman explains. What does help? Having strong core and quad muscles, plus overall endurance. This trifecta, Lichtman says, is “fundamental” to staying out of the back seat.

On the endurance front, the goal is to be as fresh after lunch as you are after breakfast, Lichtman says. “Fatigue is definitely a risk factor for ACL tears,” he says, explaining that fatigued skiers more frequently get into the back seat and sustain injuries than those who aren’t zapped. So make sure your dryland training doesn’t just focus on lifting weights: “A balance of endurance and strength training is integral for a skier preparing for ski season,” Lichtman says.

#8180. A Very Serious Story About Falling Asleep While Belaying

The East Face of Mount Temple, Canada, and the scene of this story's shenanigans. (Photo: Mitra Samavaki / Getty)

Big falls are commonplace while sport climbing and bouldering, but, in my opinion, the high alpine remains largely a safe space to take your brake hand off the rope. Why? With loose rock, aerated ice, and an often minimalist rack, falling off—even with a tight belay—usually spells disaster. A climber has every reason to follow the old “the leader cannot fall” ethos.

This old school state of mind deeply resonated with me earlier this month on a difficult alpine climb on Mount Temple in the Canadian Rockies. This 1,400-meter ice and mixed route began easily enough, with a hike up a hard-packed snow slope at 6 a.m. toward the deep cleft that marked the start. Neither my partner Rory nor I were burdened with rope management during the first hour of climbing, since our rope stayed neatly coiled in a pack.

Hundreds of meters higher, below one of the crux pitches, we flaked out our rope. Above us stood a terribly skinny pillar of ice no wider than my shoulders at its base. Blue light filtered through its entirety, a sign of its youth and untrustworthiness.

“I don’t think I should place a screw in that,” Rory decided.

I scanned the shattered quartzite behind the pillar, hoping to at least keep us attached to the mountain before Rory essentially soloed the pitch. Two nervous pitons and a shallow micro nut were all I could cobble together after 10 minutes of searching. I stomped out a waist-deep hole in the snow on the back side of the pillar and clipped into our wobbly anchor. My now four-piece anchor—plus Rory’s unshakeable climbing ability—gave us great odds of surviving his lead.

The runout pitch gave me ample opportunity to pay out slack as I pleased while munching on trail mix and rehydrating from our busy morning. After all, Rory was not allowed to fall, so he didn’t.

Falling has been a frowned-upon practice for most of climbing’s history, especially before sport climbing became popular in the 1980s. Only relatively recently, and only in some styles of climbing, have leader falls become no longer taboo—even acceptable and encouraged.

The crusty old-timer in me knows that, in any form of free climbing, it is always safer to climb to the top of a pitch without testing your equipment, be it a skinny rope, crashpad, or ice screw. This gut instinct evolved from a time when climbing gear was not completely trustworthy. Maybe you hand-stitched your quickdraw’s webbing yourself. Maybe you’d sourced your climbing protection from a hardware store. Or maybe you had tied your lead line around your waist because drop-seat harnesses hadn’t been invented yet. In this era—really only a few decades ago—your climbing ability was the first line of defense. Ropes and harnesses and removable protection served merely as dubious back-ups.

But the advent of regular whippers is a tragedy for one more reason: With newfangled belay devices, hang dogging, and constant pleas to “watch me,” belaying has become a real pain in the ass.

Nearly 12 hours later, Rory and I were still on Mount Temple. We’d topped out the ice climbing portion of the face and traversed across open snow slopes and through rock bands to a final serrated crux: the Black Towers. Countless turrets of dark limestone slice across the summit ridge of Mount Temple, creating difficult route finding even on a clear summer’s day. We were approaching midnight in November and a thick fog had choked the upper mountain. Visibility hovered around 10 meters. I had no idea where we were supposed to go.

Thankfully it was Rory’s lead again, and he was questing. Fifteen minutes ticked by as he wandered up a steep rocky groove, then another 15 of the rope unmoving. An hour passed. I clicked off my headlamp to save battery. More time passed. I figured I could tie off the rope and catch a few Zs, so I did. Sleep felt amazing. I was glad that even as we approached 24 hours on the move, Rory still knew the rules: The leader cannot fall. And the belayer gets to sleep.

I woke up to the sound of Rory’s voice. He’d been blocked by an overhang and was downclimbing. Thick, icy fog obscured our vision as I took the rack and traversed along a snow ledge looking for easier passage. The fog would sometimes lift for an instant—I’d spot a lonely star above—and I’d frantically flick my headlamp to full strength to catch a glimpse of the mountain. But before my eyes could adjust to the new sight, the fog would crash back in like a breaking wave, drowning us in uncertainty once again.

This story does not end in a climbing success. We did not ultimately find our way through the Black Towers, nor did we share a weary, satisfied hug on the summit of Mount Temple. We became lost and a little delirious on a large mountain in the middle of the night and needed to go down.

We stayed roped together as we retraced our steps through deep snow on the upper mountain. I was a little worried about triggering an avalanche, but mainly I was just exhausted. If I stumbled, I would prefer to slide 30 meters before being caught by the rope than well over a thousand into the next life.

Rory and I regrouped at an anchor I’d built in an outcrop of yellow rock. He led out across another snowfield which terminated at a gigantic notch in an otherwise sheer ridgeline. The notch marked the start of a classic ski descent, the 60-degree Aemmer Couloir, and our escape hatch. Rory trudged toward it and I paid out rope, nodding off again.

Suddenly, I was awake. I had not pooped all day, yet the kilogram of trail mix and sausage and cheese I’d downed was making a basement appearance.

“Rory! Do you need a real belay for this bit? I really need to poo,” I yelled into the fog.

I let the rope feed through the anchor, then unclipped it from my belay device and, without moving even a step away from our anchor, unloaded into the snow bank.

It would have been a disgusting mess had Rory fallen and weighted the anchor, dragging me into my own steaming waste. But he didn’t, and I made it back to civilization with both my dignity and my life intact.

#8179. Kiprun Kipsummit Race Review: We Tested the Trail Super Shoe That Won the 2026 Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

When Blandine L’Hirondel crossed the finish line first at the 2026 Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc, the buzz was not only about her record-breaking 21:54:49 but also about what shoes she was wearing. L’Hirondel is a name the trail running world knows well. Her sponsor, Kiprun, isn’t, especially in the United States. Kiprun is the running brand of Decathlon, the French sporting goods giant, and the shoe on L’Hirondel’s feet was its first carbon-plated trail racer, the Kipsummit Race.

The debut racer, also the least expensive shoe on the podium at $250, clearly held its own in a field of tried-and-proven competitors. Runner-up Rachel Entrekin’s Norda 055, for example, retails for $325. Other models on the podium ranged from $260 to $280.

For the last three months, I’ve been testing the Kiprun Kipsummit Race to find out firsthand what this new $250 trail super shoe can do.

Weight: 9 oz (men’s 8); 7.8 oz (women’s 5) Stack Height: 37.5–31.5 mm Heel-to-Toe Drop: 6 mm Lug Depth: 4 mm

+ One of the lightest carbon trail racers + Firm, responsive midsole doesn’t feel mushy + Confidence-inspiring stability and grip, especially on descents – Stiff sole and upper need a break-in period – Not ideal for very technical, rocky terrain

I was first introduced to Kiprun at The Running Event in December 2025, a trade show for run specialty retailers and brands. I was immediately drawn to the Kipsummit Race, the brand’s marquee carbon-plated trail shoe, and couldn’t wait to test it. Nearly nine months later, Blandine L’Hirondel wore it to her record-setting win at UTMB. Coincidentally (or not?), my sample pair arrived in the mail just after the win.

From the moment I picked it up, the Kipsummit Race felt remarkably light. At 9 ounces for a men’s 8 and 7.8 ounces for a women’s 5, it’s one of the lightest carbon-plated trail shoes you can buy. Fittingly, the only other shoe as lightweight is the Asics Metafuji Trail 2, which Ben Dhiman wore to win the men’s race at UTMB.

The Kipsummit Race has one of the toughest uppers I’ve tested. The patented upper material (a blend of polyester, thermoplastic polyurethane, and polyamide) is lightweight and extremely durable, with a stiff, structured feel that really holds the foot in place once the laces are cinched. It’s not the coziest feel out of the box, but over time, it broke in and felt more comfortable.

Underfoot, the ATPU midsole uses an embedded, full-length, forked carbon fiber plate to create a rigid, rockered sole. Most of the ATPU midsoles I’ve tested have been in road shoes, and tend to be very soft. The Kipsummit Race was not. The shoe felt firmer than I expected during my first test run on a crushed gravel path outside Philadelphia. That wasn’t necessarily a bad thing: It was firm, but it had a responsive pop, and I didn’t notice any sinking into the midsole or instability on stance and push-off.

On another test run in Santa Barbara, California, I climbed about 1,200 feet up a dirt fire road. It was rutted and rocky from water runoff, but the shoe remained stable on the uneven terrain. The firmer midsole, paired with a wide base, felt grounded, and the forked plate, with a cut-out under the heel, kept my foot centered. When I needed to navigate through technical terrain, however, the thick, wide profile and lack of ground feel wasn’t ideal.

The Kipsummit Race really shone on the descent. The Vibram Megagrip Litebase outsole with 4 millimeter lugs gripped loose rock and kitty litter with confidence, while still being mild enough to run on roads for long stretches. I’m not naturally a strong downhill runner, but I felt safe going beyond my comfort zone, which I attribute to the combination of great grip, a firmly stable midsole, a wide base, and a secure upper.

The one thing I didn’t get to test is how comfortable the shoe, with its firmer midsole and stiff upper, feels over ultra distances. The shoe started to break in with more use, so you may need to log more miles in it to feel its true comfort. Kiprun boasts that it holds up for more than 1,000 kilometers (about 620 miles), and given that L’Hirondel trusted one pair for the entire UTMB, that tracks.

Like carbon fiber road racing shoes, carbon fiber trail shoes have a reputation for being made only for fast, strong, competitive runners. That reputation may be earned on the road, but I don’t think it’s true for trail shoes. There isn’t nearly as much research showing that carbon fiber trail shoes provide any performance benefit to trail runners, elite or beginner—the plates function as much for protection and stability as they do for propulsion.

That said, plated trail shoes offer a different running experience than non-plated shoes. If that feels good to you, then wear them. This is my long way of saying that the Kiprun Kipsummit Race is suitable for any runner who likes a stiffer shoe, both in flex and cushioning, that holds up to high mileage. It’s best suited for smooth to moderately technical terrain, and for anything from short trail races to 100-milers.

#8178. My Local Trail Is Crumbling. Should I Fix It Without Approval?

Authorized trail work (like the work shown) is more preferable. But sometimes hikers do trail repairs on their own. (Photo: Marty Caivano/Getty Images)

What should you do when your favorite trails aren’t being maintained? The question was sparked by a recent story in the Los Angeles Times about a concerned hiker who lugged nearly 100 pounds of construction materials up Mount Baldy. The hiker proceeded to install a DIY retaining barrier to widen a crumbling section of trail across a well-known section called Devil’s Backbone in August.

According to the LA Times, the hiker is named Mark Orr. On Reddit, some commenters thanked Orr for taking the initiative to improve a popular and dangerous trail, where hikers have fallen to their deaths in the past. Others saw videos of the repairs and raised concerns. Would Orr’s project—constructed from aluminum sheeting, steel wire, and rebar—really hold up against years of erosion and heavy foot traffic?

Within just a few weeks, runoff carved a deep hole in the dirt below the retaining wall, proving the naysayers right.

“The first thing is, it was nothing but well-intentioned by somebody who loves the mountain and wants it to be safer for everybody,” Orr told the LA Times. “I totally get that my first crack at this, I didn’t do everything right, and I’m actively working with the San Gabriel Mountains Trailbuilders to get it right before this winter.”

As a longtime trail worker, I can’t condone Orr’s trail work on Mount Baldy, even if his heart was in the right place. But after years of building trails and working with volunteers, I also know that unauthorized trail work happens all the time. I’ve seen poorly constructed drainage ditches, wobbly rock staircases, and retaining walls I didn’t trust to hold my body weight.

I have also seen hikers clearing away brush, pruning branches, and cutting and then removing downed trees that have fallen across the trail. I see people with chainsaws strapped to their dirt bikes or loppers in a side pouch of their backpacks. The work these hikers, cyclists, and dirt bikers do is sometimes illegal. It’s also necessary. Without them, our trails would be in worse shape. And given the state of our public land management agencies, I can’t blame them for choosing to go rogue.

But amongst ad hoc trail work, there’s a sliding scale between harmful and helpful. And I have some thoughts on when and where it’s justified to do unsanctioned trail work. Spoiler alert: if you’re planning on building walls, moving boulders, or cutting down trees, you need to go back to the drawing board.

One of my friends, a U.S. Forest Service trail manager in Tennessee who asked not to be named in this story, has gone to great lengths to empower local citizens to perform trail work themselves. Thanks to his efforts, volunteers are now certified to use chainsaws on Forest Service land and operate independently. When they come across downed logs or a brushy trail, they don’t have to seek permission to organize a trail maintenance day. They just get to work.

Unfortunately, not every national forest has the manpower to do this. Land management agencies like the Forest Service and National Park Service are in the midst of unprecedented budget cuts and staffing shortages, and our trails are suffering. Since President Trump’s second inauguration in January 2025, the Forest Service has shed more than 5,000 jobs, including thousands of field-going employees like rangers and trail workers. An internal Forest Service report leaked last year came to a dire conclusion: “Many districts are unable to complete basic trail maintenance. Backcountry trails are being abandoned. Deferred maintenance is exponentially compounding.”

For 2027, Trump is proposing a further 44 percent cut to the Forest Service’s operations budget, which covers employee salaries. The agency has been gutted. Some forest districts no longer have even a single trail worker.

The Forest Service says that it hopes to offset these challenges through its volunteer program, which it overhauled in 2024. But the agency is now so decimated that some districts can’t even provide mandatory training to volunteers. If you’re a would-be volunteer hoping to use a chainsaw to clear your favorite Forest Service trail, you’re supposed to take a three-day training course first. But many ranger districts no longer offer chainsaw training, forcing volunteers to find a non-profit that offers a similar course, which usually means hours of travel and paying for overnight accommodations.

Despite those challenges, you should reach out to these agencies and local groups before picking up a tool and heading to the trail. In some cases, you can get in touch with the organization, or land manager, that’s legally responsible for trail maintenance, like the city, county, or state parks and recreation department. In other situations, it may be easier to contact a volunteer group that’s already connected with your local land managers.

“Contacting your local land manager or volunteer group is how you learn the basics,” Sam Donnelly, the acting executive director at the Tahoe Rim Trail Association told Outside. “It also builds goodwill and makes things official. Land managers can sign an individual volunteer agreement with you if there’s no volunteer organization in the area. All of this helps to prove that you want to show up and put in the work.”

Donnelly would know. Maintaining the 165-mile Tahoe Rim Trail is a joint effort between the organization he leads and three national forest units, a state park in Nevada, and another non-profit group—not to mention dozens of volunteers.

He understands that some people want to speed up the process by doing unsanctioned trail work. But he does not encourage it. “It’s a trust-building thing,” he said. “We didn’t get here overnight, but we have the impact we do now because we’ve done things the right way.”

Even if you’re convinced there’s no one out there maintaining your local trails, you might be pleasantly surprised. A directory of trail groups on Pinkbike  lists over 1,600 organizations in the United States. Shoot your local group an email, and chances are they’ll be happy to put you to work. In areas with established groups, it might take a while until your favorite trail or pet project makes it onto the calendar. But if you show up consistently, take classes and get first aid certified, you can likely become a trip leader and have input on which trails need attention.

In areas where trails are more remote and less trafficked, volunteer trail work is often a more casual affair. My mother, a lifetime hiker who lives in central Pennsylvania, was handed a pair of loppers and told she was in charge of maintaining a three-mile section of the Mid-State Trail—without any oversight—on her very first day as a volunteer. All it took was one email and a 15-minute demonstration, and she was official.

Even if a volunteer group in your area isn’t very active, it’s probably worth reaching out.  A group might not have enough active members to plan work trips, but could still provide valuable intel. They can connect you with land managers, loan you tools, or give you keys to unlock gates for quicker trail access. Plus, your volunteer hours may count towards them receiving a funding grant in the future.

If you’re truly unable to work with a land manager or volunteer group, I believe there are times when unauthorized trail work is the right choice, even if it is prohibited by the letter of the law.

Trail work exists on a spectrum in terms of complexity. The most complicated tasks, like building bridges, erecting retaining walls, and constructing new trails from scratch, are really engineering projects. The simplest tasks, like trimming back overgrown brush, require almost no training. Most trail work exists in a gray area between these two extremes.

Complex trail-building projects are not the place to be doing unauthorized trail work. For one thing, they’re often far more involved than most people realize. Even building a small retaining wall takes a lot of effort. The rock or lumber used in the wall generally extends far underground, and is reinforced with rebar and lag screws. The structure is filled with tons of crushed rock and dirt. Staircases, water bars, grade dips, and switchbacks are all similarly complex projects.

“Trail building, just the science of it, has come a really long way,” Donnelly said. “There’s a lot more thought put into it than you’d expect. A retaining wall is a good example. It takes weeks to build one so that it will last a hundred years. A normal person who thinks they can just go out and do trail work on their own is probably just creating more work for the people who come after.”

Even if you think you know what you’re doing, you could expose yourself to legal trouble by taking on serious trail improvements without approval. Rerouting even a small section of trail often requires an environmental review, as does building a new bridge or boardwalk. You could build a perfect retaining wall, and land managers will still remove it to comply with the rules and regulations they must follow. If you’re interested in this kind of work, you need to volunteer with an official organization.

It might not be glamorous, but the dead-simple tasks like pruning and cutting branches are really the only ones appropriate for unofficial trail work. The main reason for this is that routine maintenance doesn’t change a trail’s character. You aren’t deciding whether a new retaining wall is appropriate on a wilderness trail. You aren’t building berms for mountain bikes on a multi-use trail. You aren’t digging ditches across the trail where you think water erosion is an issue. All you’re doing is restoring the trail to what it is supposed to look like in the first place. As long as you don’t leave “punji sticks”, the sharp stubs that are created when you don’t prune a branch flush to the ground or a limb, it’s hard to go wrong. For myself, that means tossing a small hand saw or pair of loppers in my day pack when I go hiking or riding in areas where I know trail maintenance is spotty. I’ll spend an hour of my time cutting back any brush that touches my body as I walk past.

It’s boring work, and I rarely finish brushing out an entire trail before I have to move on. I don’t get the same sense of accomplishment from pruning branches as I do from moving boulders to build a staircase or cutting down trees to build a log bridge. But it’s important work, it’s hard to mess up, and no reasonable land manager would give you grief for doing it. In general, trails won’t disappear when a bridge gives out or a staircase falls apart, so long as the rest of the trail is in good condition. But if the entire length of a trail disappears under brush and downed logs, it might be abandoned entirely, or even removed from official maps. Once a trail is decommissioned, it’s far more difficult and costly to build a new trail to replace it, because new trails require lengthy environmental reviews. Simply put, if you love a trail, doing the easy, routine maintenance to make sure it remains passable is the best thing you can do.

#8177. The Terminus of the CDT is Now Behind a Border Wall. Here’s What Hikers Can Expect

The southern terminus of the Continental Divide Trail has changed a lot in the last year. The granite obelisk once stood in the open Chihuahuan Desert, in a remote area visited by few except hikers either starting or ending their journeys. The dirt road approaching it, Commodore Road, was unmaintained and required high-clearance vehicles, limiting access and traffic.

Now, though, the monument stands between two imposing 30-foot border walls currently under construction, in a National Defense Area (NDA). Government contractors graded and widened the road from 8 feet to 24 feet to accommodate construction vehicles. For now, hikers can still enter the NDA with permission and touch the monument—whether they’re starting northbound or ending their CDT hike. However, security guards will eventually usher them away, out of the construction zone.

In November, Teresa Martinez, the executive director of the CDT Coalition (CDTC), and Audra Labert, the CDTC director of communications, traveled to the southern terminus. Neither had been there since construction began in early 2026.

“We wanted to see on the ground what was actually happening and what people were experiencing,” Martinez told Backpacker. She described the scene as “surreal.”

Arriving at the terminus monument, Martinez and Labert watched as two hikers approached in the distance. The two women, trail names Geisha Girl and Fearless, marched toward them, border walls standing on both sides. In an emotional moment, the teary-eyed hikers walked right up to the monument.

“I think if they hadn’t been able to put their hands on the physical monument, even though it was between the two barriers, it would have been devastating,” Martinez said. “The importance of having access to that now while it’s under construction is so fundamental.”

While these changes are striking to someone like Martinez, who has visited this terminus hundreds of times during her work with the non-profit trail organization, she says she sees a silver lining. The construction traffic is annoying, loud, disruptive, and changes the experience of finishing or starting your CDT hike in a quiet corner of the desert. But the improvements to Commodore Road greatly increase access to the trail’s southern terminus.

“Building a road invites more people, which means more people can get there, which is a beautiful thing. They can drive their loved ones to the trail and pick them up from the trail much easier than it ever has been,” she said. But at the same time, the improvements make it feel less remote, and could make it significantly busier. “So it’s bittersweet,” she said.

Sometime “in the near future,” Martinez said the terminus monument will be moved out of the NDA. Then, the CDTC will create a new one with accurate longitude and latitude markers. She sees that as an opportunity to rethink how the monument will be dedicated and to include indigenous voices that weren’t involved when the original monument was dedicated in 1974.

Asked what hikers should expect when approaching the southern terminus of the CDT, Martinez paused thoughtfully.

“I think they should be prepared for an amazing experience in one of the most beautiful places on the planet,” she said. “But you’re going to see this infrastructure now that didn’t exist before. And I would ask people to lean into the good stuff and then also use that moment as an opportunity to reflect on how the experience is making them feel.”

#8176. Put Your Rock Shoes in the Oven—You’ll Thank Us

A pinhole image of a person peering into their oven at home. (Photo: Getty Images)

I grew up in a gym. I learned my first curse words on a chalky, sweat-stained gym mat. I got my first tattoo with the friends I did four-by-fours with. First boyfriend, even.

If there’s one thing that has held true over my years of cramming my feet into tiny, downturned rock shoes for the sake of performance, it’s that breaking in shoes sucks. Every time, no getting around it, a horrible experience. During one gym session, a friend said she’d pay to have someone break in her shoes for her. We were the same size, and I was pretty desperate for money at the time—but still, some things just aren’t worth it. And when you not only have to break in the shoes, but have a double training session ahead of you while your feet are screaming with pain? I’m sure that I cried once over it.

When the pandemic hit, suddenly I wasn’t going to the gym anymore. And because—at least at the beginning—nobody was sure about transmission via holds outside, I refrained from climbing rock as well. During that turbulent time, a funny thing happened: Either my feet flattened out or my tolerance for tiny shoes decreased. Because when gyms reopened and I tried to push myself through the break-in process again, suddenly it felt a lot more hateful.

As I complained loudly (and probably all while looking desperate) at Monkey House Carbondale in December 2020, a local friend, the pro climber Dan Mirsky, overheard me.

“No way. They’ll delaminate!” I protested.

“No, seriously. Just for a few minutes on the lowest setting. Game-changer.”

I took his tip, which I later learned he had originally gotten from another pro climber, Jonathan Siegrist, to heart. That night, I set up my station: oven, on the lowest setting (170 degrees), timer, and area on the carpet where I would dance around like a circus monkey. In the shoes went, for two minutes. I would then wear them for five to ten minutes—pacing, with some good ol’ fashioned calf raises mixed in—and then they’d go back in the oven, for another cycle or two. (Note: This only works with a standard oven, not a microwave—do not microwave your rock shoes or it will severely damage/deform them!)

I couldn’t believe the results. Those brand-new puppies felt more akin to the pair you sweated in all summer and have yet to send to a resoler (God bless the person who has to touch that pair). It was one of those moments when you realize your life has changed forever.

And a fun fact for you, which I learned with more research: Leather stretches when wet (duh!). So try the oven thing, plus adding a sprinkling of water when they shoes are still hot, prior to donning them. And voilà! Your warm, wet shoes will slide right on and stretch even more.

Curious for his take, I reached out to Siegrist. “Yes, I do that sometimes!” he wrote. “Not as much any more, because I think I just simply get bigger shoes. Ha!”

And that, actually, might just be the best tip of all.

Note: While the author has successfully applied this tip on multiple occasions, as has Siegrist and Mirsky, not all shoemakers recommend. Scarpa, for example, has noted that this method of breaking in shoes will reduce glue strength and void shoe warranty.

#8175. The 9 Best Hiking Towns to Spend Your Holidays In

(Photo: Photos from Terry's photostream via Flickr Creative Commons)

But not everyone can access hiking right out their front door. So why not turn your holiday break into a hiking vacation? You’ll not only get to make special festive memories outside, but you can choose the geography and even the climate.

With that in mind, we’ve put together a list of the best places for hikers to holiday. Want to spend your time traipsing through deserts, among cacti and palm trees? We’ve got you covered. Looking for a more traditional experience, with snowy trails and evergreen forests? No problem. And, of course, if you like long walks on the beach and among tropical rainforests, we’ve got just the places for you.

Why it’s a great holiday town: Mild weather, southwestern culture, diverse landscapes, and amazing food December temps: 40-65℉ What to expect: Both desert and mountain landscapes with rocky, sandy terrain, and no snow

For those hikers who’d rather decorate a saguaro cactus than a lodgepole pine, Tucson, Arizona is calling your name. The wildernesses around town are packed with desert flora and fauna, and crisscrossed with tons of hiking trails. This can be a tough place to explore during late spring, summer, and even into fall because it gets so scorching hot. However, in the winter, the weather is perfect for hiking, making this a prime place to spend the holidays. Beyond the trails, the food is world-renowned—Tucson has been a UNESCO City of Gastronomy for over a decade.

Why it’s a great holiday town: Fair weather, proximity to Gila National Forest and Cliff Dwellings Monument, colorful western history, and a great art scene December temps: 21-55℉ What to expect: Colder, high desert climate, with very clear weather, and tons of trails exploring the Pinos Altos and Mogollon Mountains

Situated on the outskirts of the Gila National Forest, Silver City is a gateway to desert hiking adventures. The Continental Divide Trail passes nearby; City of Rocks State Park is just 30 miles east of town, and the famous Gila Cliff Dwellings National Monument is just 44 miles north. The monument area gets over 200 cloudless nights a year, making it a prime destination for winter stargazers. If you want a warm soak after your hikes, Faywood Hot Springs and Gila Hot Springs are both close to town.

Why it’s a great holiday town: Mild temperatures, direct access to Zion National Park, regional access to Bryce Canyon or Grand Canyon, and a lively restaurant and art scene December temps: 30-55℉ What to expect:  A striking red sandstone desert landscape and trails both in the park and outside of it

Winter is Zion National Park’s slow season, and yet it’s just as beautiful as it is any other time of year. Springdale sits just outside the park’s eastern entrance and is a prime location for a hiking holiday basecamp. Not only will you have direct access to the national park and all of its trails, but there are also worthy routes around town that don’t require an entrance fee. And if you aren’t afraid of a day trip, Bryce Canyon is 86 miles away.

Why it’s a great holiday town: Mild temperatures, access to Lake Mead, fun holiday atmosphere, and a historic downtown December temps: 35-55℉ What to expect: Wide Mojave desert terrain with rolling hills and rocky mountains, canyons, panoramic lake views, and old mining and railroad infrastructure

The deserts of southern Nevada have a lot to offer beyond the flashing lights, casinos, and nightlife of Las Vegas. About an hour southeast of Sin City, Boulder City is a much quieter historic town that offers access to some amazing trails and outdoor recreation areas. It’s just a short drive from Boulder City to Lake Mead Recreation Area, where there are a lot of trails, walkways, and observation points. Some hikes close to town are short and approachable, while others challenge hikers with scrambles and steep climbs. The city itself is full of history; it was once an old mining town and played an important role in the Hoover Dam’s construction.

Why it’s a great holiday town: Mountain scenery and trails, access to Blue Ridge Parkway, and relatively mild temperatures and weather December temps: 35-55℉ What to expect: Forested mountains, waterfalls, and (potentially) snowy trails

Within minutes of Asheville, you’ll find waterfall hikes, mountain overlooks, and plenty of access to public lands. The Blue Ridge Mountains make a beautiful backdrop for town, and an even more spectacular place to explore by trail. Asheville’s thickly wooded forests are magical to hike, with trails following icy creeks and ascending ridges to spectacular views. After your hike, the town is renowned for its craft beer scene and festive holiday light displays. If a cozy Appalachian holiday is your vibe, look no further.

Why it’s a great holiday town: Situated high in the Rocky Mountains, lively restaurant and bar scene, trails in every direction, and close to two ski resorts December temps: 12-42℉ What to expect: Cold-weather mountain hikes, snowy trails, old-growth forests, and high desert terrain

Durango, Colorado, is a pure western mountain ski town and a genuinely cozy place to spend the holidays. The San Juan Mountains offer incredible hiking for all levels, whether you just want to stroll along a creek or climb for panoramic views of the Rockies. This region gets a lot of snow in the wintertime, so be prepared for cold weather with the right gear, knowledge, and expectations. For holiday adventurers, Durango is packed with things to do in the winter. Beyond the hiking trails, ride the historic Durango and Silverton Narrow Gauge Railroad, or go skiing at Wolf Creek or Purgatory Resorts.

Why it’s a great holiday town: Warm, subtropical winter weather, surrounded by ample inland and beach hiking, and deeply historic roots December temps: 50-70℉ What to expect: Sand dune beaches, flatland ecosystems, wetlands, and marshes

St. Augustine offers a unique take on the traditional winter holiday. It’s coastal, subtropical, and offers landscapes and ecosystems you’ll only find in Florida—from swamp conservation areas to beach parks and historic forts. There are over 30 trails and walkways around St. Augustine, and it’s within an hour’s drive of six state parks. Most of the hiking is very approachable, following beaches, boardwalks, sand dunes, and mostly flat terrain. The town was settled over 450 years ago, so it’s also a great place for history buffs, and it annually hosts a Christmas parade and “Night of Lights” throughout December.

Why it’s a great holiday town: Warm, tropical weather, dramatic natural scenery, laid-back island culture, and great hiking access December temps: 65-80℉ What to expect: Lush rainforests, beautiful beaches, mountains spouting waterfalls, and the opportunity to surf big swells

Hawaii is a famous holiday destination for obvious reasons. In the winter, the climate is pleasant; the landscape is dramatic, there are beaches a’plenty, and the hiking access is hard to beat. Waterfalls spout from the mountains, and trails wind through thick rainforest, popping out on beaches that you might have all to yourself. Hanalei, on Kauai’s North Shore, offers some of Hawaii’s best (and most diverse) hiking. Nearby are several forest reserves, Kōke’e State Park, and the Hanalei National Wildlife Refuge.

Why it’s a great holiday town: Bavarian influence, Christmas spirit, and ample winter trails to explore December temps: 15-35℉ What to expect: Snowy trails through old-growth forests and mountains, and a town that really loves to celebrate Christmas

Tucked away in the Cascade Mountains of Washington, along the Wenatchee River, this Bavarian-influenced town is one of the best places to spend the holidays on this list. The hiking in the surrounding mountains offers access to postcard-worthy alpine lakes, waterfalls, and ridges. It ranges from strenuous and challenging to easy and mellow. You’ll want snowshoes and/or microspikes if you plan on holidaying in Leavenworth, as the trails will likely be snowy and/or icy in places. The town is well-known for its Christmas zeal: It has a “Christmastown,” a Bavarian village that comes to life with live music, carols, ice carving, fireworks, and, of course, appearances by Santa Claus.

#8174. The Best Spots to Choose-and-Cut Your Own Christmas Tree This Year

You know the scene from National Lampoon’s Christmas Vacation. Clark Griswold, played by comedian Chevy Chase, is on a quest to provide an unforgettable holiday for his family when he leads his less-than-enthused wife and kids into the snowy woods, his eyes gleaming with excitement. He’s on a mission to find the Christmas tree of all Christmas trees. This classic holiday movie is almost 40 years old, but the drive to cut down your own tree is still very much alive today.

While you cannot simply waltz into any forest and begin chopping down trees, you can absolutely fulfill your dreams of being your own Clark Griswold this festive season. Instead of buying a tree from a lot in town, choose-and-cut Christmas tree farms and a special U.S. Forest Service permit program allow you to do as the name suggests: find your own tree and cut it down yourself.

These permits range from $5 to $20, and they’re as much of a win for the woods as for those wanting an authentic Clark Griswold experience.

“In the West, one of our biggest challenges is wildfire risk,” Marcus Selig, chief conservation officer for the National Forest Foundation, tells Outside. “When you’re cutting a Christmas tree [through this permit program], you’re cutting out the small trees that create what we call ladder fuel, so thinning out those little trees and allowing the big trees to have the resources they need to grow bigger and stronger and more fire resilient is good.”

Selig says this thinning out trees is something the National Forest Foundation and U.S. Forest Service spends thousands of dollars per-acre to accomplisheach year, so allowing people to cut Christmas trees helps that cause. Cutting down smaller trees can also help improve wildlife habitat and the other trees around it.

“With climate concerns, trees are more and more stressed as we go through droughts,” Selig explains. “Cutting out the small trees is like weeding a garden and means the big trees can do better.”

Some choose-and-cut farms also lean into sustainability using a regenerative farming method called coppicing, where a portion of the tree’s trunk and a branch or two are left after it’s cut down, stimulating new growth. A new tree can sprout up from the same trunk and can do so over and over again.

“We have a few stumps that you can see where they’ve been regrown at least nine times,” Christy Carico, farm manager at Crest Ranch Tree Farm in Santa Cruz, California, tells Outside. Carico refers to the method, one her family uses on their farm, as “stump culture.”

For your own choose-and-cut adventure, these eight spots have plenty of holiday cheer and even more fir, cypress, pine, and spruce Christmas trees, among other varieties, to choose from. Just double-check your ceiling heights before you head out, and check for any pesky stowaway squirrels before bringing your tree home.

Roughly 300,000 people participate in this true Clark Griswold experience—the U.S. Forest Service Christmas Tree Permit Program—each season, a program that requires you to trek into a national forest, choose and cut your tree with a hand saw, and haul it back to your car on your own.

Pay attention to the areas each forest has designated for this program, and select a tree that will help thin out the forest, not one that’s standing alone.

Selig recommends strapping the tree on top of your car with the trunk closest to the front windshield to get it home. That way, the wind will flow with the direction the branches are lying, reducing any potential for damage.

“It’s amazing what trees can take,” Selig says. “They’re made to withstand strong winds in the wild, so they’ll be all right.”

What’s the best benefit of opting for a choose-and-cut Christmas tree? “You know exactly where your tree came from and know it’s fresh,” says Tim Nieman, COO for the John T. Nieman Nursery. “These trees will last way longer than a tree you buy at a lot that’s been pre-cut probably one or two months ago.”

About 5,000 families tromp through this choose-and-cut Christmas tree farm about 30 minutes north of Cincinnati during the holidays. You can fell your own tree or have one of the team members, likely one of the roughly 25 Nieman family members who help out for the season, do it.

Red Barn Tree Farm has 40 acres of Fraser fir Christmas trees and sits adjacent to Linville Falls Winery near Boone, North Carolina. The Wiseman family has owned the property since 1998 and has always operated a choose-and-cut farm on it. In 2012, they opened the winery’s tasting room.

“Our family joke is that we always encourage customers to pick their tree first before they visit the winery next door, or else their ceilings start getting taller,” says co-owner Lindsay Wiseman.

Hop on a hayride from the base of the farm up the hill to start your search. After choosing the perfect tannenbaum, their team will do the honors of cutting it down.

Shell’s Christmas Tree Farm grows eight different tree varieties across 20 acres, including the blue ice cypress and Virginia pine, and has been selling trees for four decades. All of these species are able to grow in warmer weather as opposed to popular Christmas tree varieties like the Fraser fir, which need much cooler temperatures to thrive.

The farm typically doesn’t officially open until close to Thanksgiving, but eager customers can go ahead and visit to tag their dream tree before the season starts for a small fee.

Maple Row Farm is a family-owned and run choose-and-cut farm that has been growing Christmas trees for over 100 years. Now, according to general manager and ninth-generation farmer Scott Edwards, the 250-acre farm has a “few hundred thousand trees” at any given time. They grow nine different varieties, from white spruce trees to Fraser fir and Norway spruce trees.

During the holiday season, the farm is as known for its tailgating as it is for its trees. It’s a quirky tradition that’s just as much a must-do for customers as is choosing their own tree. “People come and bring their neighborhood, or sports team, or friends,” Edwards says. “They’ll make food and usually bring a good selection of drinks as well. It’s different, but a cool thing.”

Choose-and-cut Christmas trees are only part of the allure of Spring Creek Growers, a southeast Texas family-owned farm. Plan on making a day trip out of it if you have little ones; the epic treehouse and hayrides are must-dos, and you can buy s’mores kits from the on-site bakery to make over one of their outdoor fire pits.

During the holidays, the farm offers experiences such as doughnuts with Santa[[,]]and Tinsel and Tackle, a fishing experience for the littles.

Everything is bigger in Texas, and the same goes for Spring Creek’s trees: this year, customers can find Christmas trees up to 13 feet tall to take home.

The Rocks Christmas Tree Farm sits on 1,400 acres that were gifted to the Society for the Protection of New Hampshire Forests in 1978, with the condition that the land always be used for crops. When Nigel Manley, senior outreach manager for The Rocks and a farmer himself, started working there in 1986, it was a dairy farm. But it transitioned to growing trees shortly after he arrived.

“We decided on choose-and-cut Christmas trees as the crop because it would bring people to a conserved property,” Manley says. They used to plant 7,000 new trees a year, but Manley says warmer and wetter conditions as a result of climate change have meant scaling back to just 2,000. Keeping the former scale would have meant needing extensive field drainage or building raised beds.

Any profits from tree sales go back into things like educational programs and conservation efforts for the society.

California’s oldest Christmas tree farm, Crest Ranch, has been operating since 1948 and has been owned by the same family all 70-plus years. It’s such a beloved part of the community that even in the wake of the devastating CZU Lightning Complex wildfire that swept through the Santa Cruz Mountains in 2020 and destroyed much of the property, people still came to buy their trees.

“We were about to throw in the towel,” Carico says, “but our customers pushed us through post-fire and came that year and bought burnt trees to show their support.”

The farm has started to recover, but there are still sections of their fields that will remain closed this season, limiting how many trees they’ll be able to sell. Post-fire, Carico and her team planted a host of Monterey fir trees, endemic to the area and a fast-growing variety, but customers will also find species like white firs and Arizona cypresses available.

Washington is known as “The Evergreen State” due to its abundant forests, making it a natural spot for Christmas trees to shine. There are a number of national forests across the state, including Olympic, Gifford Pinchot, and Mount Baker-Snoqualmie, that offer Christmas tree permits if you’re feeling up for a walk in the woods.

If not, there is an abundance of U-pick farms, too. Buttonwood Farm says they are the state’s only 100 percent certified organic Christmas tree farm and that they don’t use any chemicals to manage the farm.

You can schedule an appointment to choose and cut your tree, but walk-ins are also welcome. For the ultimate experience, you can go to the farm, pick the perfect tree, and then have their team deliver it to your house.

#8173. The Six Formative Moments in Every Climbing Career

Placing your first cam is a memorable, and often horrifying, moment in every climber's career. (Photo: Andrew Burr)

Every climber has experienced a truly unforgettable moment. For some, it’s tagging that tree after climbing the Nose. For others, it’s the vast bulk of Denali filling the windshield of the de Havilland Otter. For yet others still, it’s that first splitter at Indian Creek, that first wide crack at Vedauwoo, or that first roof at the Shawangunks.

Not all climbers will share these exact memories, but there are some key moments that define almost every climbing career. Whether you’re a climber from Southern California or from Northern Vietnam, these will probably be familiar, and they probably changed the way you do business. They’re rites of passage, and when newer climbers pass through those same gates, you’ll grin knowingly, nod your head and say “Shit, we’ve all been there!”

These days, just about every climber gets started indoors, and the transition from gym to crag is a big deal. When you tentatively emerge from the womb of the climbing gym, the possibilities of ascending ACTUAL ROCKS are infinite and exhilarating. There you are with your laminated lead card still attached to your harness, squinting and blinking in the unfamiliar sunlight, craning your neck ever upward under a vast sea of stone…

On closer inspection, you see them—occasionally chalked, but devoid of color, tape, or any visual aid that would denote a route. This is concerning, and your consternation only deepens as you pull on. What follows is a desperate pumpfest during which you grasp ineffectively at every possible (and impossible) hold, ignore your footwork, and mutter phrases like “Is this one on?” and “5.9, my ass.”

Now, I realize that several crusty veterans are about to flood the comments section with hardcore tales from the pre-gym era—how the closest they’ve ever come to touching plywood was hammering home-slung timber chocks into cracks, how much of the Earth’s granite was still cooling in subterranean caverns when they started climbing, how their favorite Triceratop died of exhaustion during a regular 16-day approach. Sure, not every climbing career began with a heady gym to crag transition, but the impertinent youths whose did would agree—we’ve all been there.

You’re inching left on a sketchy traverse when your belayer blasts you with an unsolicited beta spray.

“Watch that rope, dude. It’s behind your leg.”

But you don’t got this, and when your foot pops and that tenuous crimp unlatches, you fall. The rope catches mid-calf and suddenly you’re upside-down and giving the wall the old “Glasgow Kiss”—a headbutt, in other words. Wear a helmet, kids. After righting yourself and lowering to the ground, it’s not entirely clear what hurts more: that throbbing, rope-shaped welt fused with tiny purple and yellow fibers or your pride.

Nope, it’s definitely your pride, but you can salve your damaged ego with the knowledge that almost every climber suffers the indignity of a super-ugly-upside-down-leg-behind-the-rope whipper at some point. Most will only suffer it once, because this hard-knock lesson improves rope management which makes for better, safer lead climbing. Don’t feel too bad, you’re not alone in making this rookie mistake. We’ve all been there.

It might happen on that 5.9 you’ve climbed more times than you’ve had hot dinners, or perhaps on the tail end of a 12-hour minor epic. Either way, as you prepare to lower or rappel, you notice that something is not quite right. Scratch that—it’s horrifically wrong. You’re not clipped in properly, and had you have weighted the system, you’d have taken the Big Ride.

In the days and weeks following this potentially fatal near-miss, make a serious review of your systems. The experience should form a powerful lesson—almost as powerful as the gastro-intestinal evacuations that occurred after the bad taco you ate in El Potrero Chico.

Complacency and fatigue are often factors, but the true reason for serious human error is this: Your systems suck. Maybe you’re weren’t applying best practice, or maybe you’re not consistent enough with those that you do use. A smart (or sufficiently chastened) climber will embrace this opportunity to analyze, criticize, and ultimately improve techniques, because although we’ve all been there, it’s not somewhere we wish to return.

There comes a time in a climber’s life when they must place a piece of traditional protection, either by design or by default. Then comes a sudden realization, a piercing moment when it becomes clear that one’s entire being is committed to the inner workings of a spring-loaded camming device or the security of an asymmetrical hunk of aluminum. Eyes glaze over, total recall of high school physics occurs, Rainman-esque calculations of friction coefficients and force vectors take place…

This moment is polarizing. It alternately fills climbers with invigoration, or with an existential dread so profound it would make Friedrich Nietzsche look like the Dalai Lama. Climbers then find themselves in one of two camps—either “newly minted trad climber” or “fuck that, never again.” And whichever camp you find yourself in, you’ll probably come to regard the other as having serious and incurable mental deficiencies. But no matter which side of the fence you end up on, we’ve all been there.

What was that? Oh, nothing. Just your A2 pulley disintegrating, along with your dreams of onsighting The Widowmaker (VI 5.14a X A4 M10ish) at HardBastard Canyon this year. Worse still, it happened in the gym. Oh, the humanity.

Your first climbing injury comes with two realizations. The first is that your immediate future is going to look a lot different from how you envisaged it five minutes ago. The second is that you’re not invincible. Everybody thinks it can’t happen to them, until it does.

The recovery period for a finger injury is horrifically tedious—six ponderous months of pulling ever so gently on holds that are no smaller than the West Buttress of Denali. Afterward, you won’t be able to tear the skin off a custard, but you’ll be a gun at warming up, an ace at stretches, and an absolute legend at taking rest days. But here’s an idea… why not buck the trend and start doing these BEFORE you get injured? We’ve all been there, but if we can prevent it from happening, why do we all wait until it’s too late?

Belayers are a dime a dozen, but a real climbing partner is a true gift. But what makes a real partner?

A real partner is just as stoked as you are, if not more so. They don’t say things like “why” and “how much.” They say things like “hell yes” and “let’s do this.” They can spoon you in a bivvy cave without it getting overly weird. They will empty your piss bottle on the understanding that you’ll return the favor sometime. They will lend you that No. 6 without a moment’s hesitation. They really, really want to see you crush that pitch.

Put simply, a real climbing partner is someone you would follow to the ends of the earth, and regularly do. A real climbing partner can turn a bad climb into a good one, a good climb into a great one, and a great climb into a life-changing experience. Forming deep and genuine connections is one of the finest aspects of the sport, and if there is one thing I truly hope, it’s that we’ve all been there.

#8172. The Next Frontier of Adventure Travel Isn’t More Adventure—It’s Better Recovery. Here’s Where to Stay.

(Photo: L to R: Four Seasons Resort Maui; Auberge Collection; Tordrillo Mountain Lodge. Design: Ayana Underwood/Canva )

As much as outdoor enthusiasts enjoy spending time in nature and nurturing their bodies and minds, it’s easy to lose space for rest while chasing the next thrill. But not anymore, as recent reports say travelers are consciously seeking experiences that balance adventure with restoration.

According to Hilton’s “The Great Rebalance: How Travelers Are Expecting to Reset and Recalibrate in 2027” survey, which surveyed 14,744 travelers across 14 countries, 65 percent of survey respondents actively book vacations that calm the body and reset the nervous system, and 79 percent say that fresh air and being outdoors help them relax when they travel.

The Global Wellness Institute’s 2026 Wellness Tourism Initiative Trends report stated that, in today’s overstimulating world, “wellness travel is increasingly shifting from performance-driven wellness toward nervous system regulation.” Booking.com said in its 11th Annual Travel Predictions report that they expect 2027 to be the era of recovery-maxxing.

All this to say, if you’re ready to book a gorgeous getaway brimming with wellness benefits, we’re here to help. The stays on this list are a bit of a splurge, but they do include an array of rejuvenating amenities in beautiful places. (They’re listed from least to most expensive based on current room rates.) That said, read ahead for five U.S. destinations that ace recovery travel.

Four Seasons Resort Maui at Wailea has drawn guests to its picture-perfect Wailea shores since opening in 1990 as the brand’s first tropical resort. For decades, the oceanfront resort has been world-renowned as a best-in-class property across accommodations, food, beverage, and hospitality. As of July 2026, next-gen wellness has been added to the list. With the opening of Kai Holo Spa, the resort’s warm, circadian-lit wellness sanctuary (where the lighting is built to regulate guests’ sleep-wake cycles to induce relaxation), guests are invited to zen out on island time, whether amongst the aquathermal circuit, with a Pacific Journeys massage in an open-air massage hale by the ocean, or at the adjoining Next|Health Longevity Clinic, where a hyperbaric chamber and IV therapies await.

You can book your stay here for a minimum of $880 per night.

For a more landlocked wellness experience, head to Texas Hill Country to explore the expansive grounds of Canyon Ranch Austin, where a 27,000-square-foot training center and recovery lab called The Barn welcomes guests to nurture their health with the help of a gym and outdoor field. The resort also includes a sprawling 40,000-square-foot spa, making it the largest spa in Texas, that offers an array of vitality treatments, from zero-gravity neurostimulation (for improved sleep and focus) and red light beds (to reduce training fatigue and pain) to an Ammortal Chamber. The Ammortal Chamber combines both red and near-infrared light, pulsed electromagnetic field (PEMF) therapy that sends electromagnetic waves through the body to ease sore muscles, molecular hydrogen, vibroacoustic sound, and guided breathwork to boost relaxation and rebalance the nervous system. Beyond that, Canyon Ranch Austin’s Women’s Wellness Collective is a dedicated women’s wellness practice that addresses hormonal therapy, brain health, sleep, perimenopause, menopause, and more.

You can book your stay here at a minimum of $1,325 per night (per person) with the Stay Your Way package. There’s a two-night minimum stay. Unlimited meals and snacks are included, along with transportation to and from Austin-Bergstrom International Airport or Horseshoe Bay Resort Airport. With this package, you’ll also receive a $200 nightly spa and fitness credit per person. If you stay three or more nights, you’ll get a $300 health and wellness credit.

Dunton Hot Springs is a romantic, rustic-luxe resort set in an 1800s ghost town. Nestled in Colorado’s San Juan Mountains, Dunton Hot Springs draws on its geography for its wellness offerings. The Wellness in the San Juans workshop is a guided two-hour workshop that combines breathwork, meditation, and mobility to deepen the connection between body and mind. Other ways to recover at the resort include soaking in the 85 degrees Fahrenheit to 106 degrees Fahrenheit calcium bicarbonate waters (which are meant to improve skin health and circulation) in the Bathhouse or under the stars in nature, healing sound baths, facials and massages, and individual, couple’s, and group yoga.

You can book your stay here. There’s a two-night minimum stay, and rates are $1,415 per night. For example, the Echo Cabin, your most affordable option, includes a 252-square-foot cabin, mountain views, a half-bath, and a secluded outdoor shower. If you’re not in the mood to shower in nature, you’re just a short walk from the bathhouse.

The Lodge at Blue Sky, only minutes from Park City, approaches recovery from a different angle, leaning into energy healing and alignment. Meander through a beautiful aspen grove into The Edge Sanctuary, a luxury glamping tent where the resort’s energy healers lead intuitive energy journeys, mesmerizing sound baths, and heart-opening tea ceremonies. For a more traditional recovery experience, pop up to The Edge Spa for indulgent facials and massages overlooking Alexander Creek. The Lodge at Blue Sky guests can also invigorate their senses with contrast therapy, where heat improves circulation and cold therapy supports muscle recovery after athletic pursuits.

You can book your stay here. Current rates start at around $1,924 per night for the 570-square-foot King Sky room, which offers one king bed, a mountain view, a 115-square-foot terrace,  and a soaking tub.

If you want to explore recovery practices without neglecting your passion for adrenaline-fueled adventure, Alaska’s Tordrillo Mountain Lodge is calling. The remote, all-inclusive luxury adventure lodge incorporates helicopters into much of its programming, from heli-skiing to the new, first-of-its-kind heli-sauna: the AlpenSauna. Earlier this year, the lodge introduced the AlpenSauna, a fly-in, custom-built sauna that the Tordrillo team moves throughout the Tordrillo Mountain Range. For example, the sauna may be positioned next to an alpine waterfall one month and in the middle of a 28-mile ice field on the Triumvirate Glacier the next. Earlier in 2026, the lodge also debuted a 2,400-square-foot wellness and recovery center co-designed by athletes, guides, and longevity experts.

Again, helicopter rides are baked into these experiences; the pricing isn’t cheap, so it is certainly a splurge. For a seven-night stay, the Winter package (February to April) costs $18,500 per person (or $2,643 per night). For a five-night stay with the Kings and Corn package (June), the package costs $16,000 per guest (or $3,200 per night). The least expensive stay comes in their Summer package (July to September). For instance, their “Season of the Salmon” package, which runs from August 13, 2027 to September 13, 2027, costs $10,500 per person (or $3,500 per night) for a Friday-to-Monday, three-night stay. In the summer, unlimited lodge activities include wake surfing, wakeboarding, stand-up paddleboarding, kayaking, and more.

You can view a comprehensive list of all packages here.

Want more Outside health stories? Sign up for the Bodywork newsletter. And for tips on how to train, fuel, and recover better, sign up for the Sweat Science 101 newsletter.

#8171. The Gear That Backpacker’s Editors Loved in November 2026

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Fall often seems to happen all at once in the Front Range of Colorado: One day it’s sunny and pushing 70, the next the leaves are falling off the trees, and the day after that it’s suddenly snowing. While it can make it tough to make plans, it also means November is a great time here for hikers who love variety.

This month, our editors backpacked the Utah desert, took in the fall foliage in the Pacific Northwest, and (finally) broke out our skis again in the Colorado mountains. From a carbon-fiber encased power pack to a gravity filter, this gear helped us do it.

Of all the viral gear I’ve seen during my tenure as a Backpacker editor, the Haribo power bank had to be the funniest. At roughly 9 ounces, the 20,000mAh battery was briefly one of the lightest batteries of its capacity on the market; all of a sudden, gram-counters were scrambling to get their hands on a gadget with a smiling cartoon bear on the side.

If you missed your chance with the Candy Battery, the NB10000 is the next best thing. At 4.94 ounces, this carbon-fiber sheathed power bank is about half the size (and half the capacity) of the Haribo one, and has a handful of nice tricks built in. Besides the standard stuff like fast charging, the NB10000 features technicolor lights built around the dual USB-C charging ports, which make it easy to find in a dark tent. At a rating of IPX7, it’s also waterproof enough to survive full immersion, making it a solid choice for paddling trips or rainy trails. One minor gripe: I found an included short USB cord handy, but it bit the dust within a few months. —Adam Roy, Editor-in-Chief

This is the first fleece on the market made with Polartec’s new, hotly-anticipated second generation Alpha fabric. So what’s the big deal? Polartec claims that this new Alpha is just as warm and breathable as the older version, while being more durable and resistant to shedding. Patagonia’s pullover does feel significantly different than the old Alpha. While the underlying scaffolding looks the same, the new fabric’s texture is more like a furry shag rug than the original tufted style.

Over several weeks of testing, it’s proven less prone to snagging on things and disintegrating in the wash. Fit-wise, the Patagonia Pullover has a casual, boxy silhouette more meant for around town wear (a bit of an odd application for Alpha.) One caveat: The fabric weight of this pullover is quite heavy—roughly 165 GSM—compared to the usual 60-90 found on ultralight Alpha hoodies. To make a proper breathability and warmth comparison, we’ll need to wait until one of the smaller cottage brands releases a lightweight version. —Benjamin Tepler, Senior Gear Editor

When it comes to hiking fashion, I tend to care a lot more about function than form. (No shade to the backpackers out there leaning into trendy apparel; the gorpcore wave is real.) That said, it’s nice to feel good on the trail, and these pants from Skida bring a pop of pure fun to my wardrobe. Lightweight, high-waisted, and flowy, the Viska comes in five of Skida’s signature colorful prints. (If you really want to get vibrant, pair them with a matching hat or buff.) They’re both the boldest and the most comfortable pants I own; the stretch polyester/lycra blend feature a wide leg and moisture-wicking properties. Wearing them feels similar to staying in my PJs all day long, minus the fashion faux pas. With UPF 50+ protection, they’re also a good choice for scorchingly bright days.

Because the fabric is so lightweight, these aren’t my go-to for actual trail miles; instead, I love to wear them lounging around camp, on long travel days, or to change into at the trailhead after a grimy hike. And I’m almost guaranteed to get a compliment or two when I wear them in public, which doesn’t hurt. —Zoe Gates, Senior Editor

I only recently got on the gravity filter train, and it’s been a paradigm shifter for me. When I get to camp, I can fill the reservoir, hang it up, and have a faucet of filtered water at the ready. On hut trips, in the winter, it’s awesome for an extra level of filtration, removing sediment and particulates from melted, boiled snow water. The Seeker Gravity Filter in particular has really won me over. Not only can I hang it up, but it has a handle on the side that allows me to hold it and use it like a regular squeeze filter.

The filter itself is a .2 micron hollow fiber filter that’s good for up to 1,500 liters of filtered water. According to Hydrapak, it catches 99.999% of bacteria, cysts, and sediment. The specs claim it filters at a rate of one liter per minute—I feel like it’s slightly slower than that, but my filter might just need a good reverse flush. Unfortunately, the original is no longer available, so you’ll have to buy the Seeker filter kit, which includes an extra reservoir for storing your filtered water. —Will Brendza, Associate Editor

#8170. 9 Moments and Pioneers From the Evolution of Yosemite, in Photos

Perhaps the most recognizable feature of the granite behemoth that is El Capitan is the gigantic diorite streak running right up the middle of the southeast face. Saped like the North American continent, it’s this route’s namesake. Although this birthmark is visually striking, the brittle black rock it contains and the lack of a clear, natural line kept climbers focused on the more aesthetic and relatively easier southwest face.

It wasn’t until October 1963 when Royal Robbins and Glen Denny began hunting around on the wall. Eventually, they aided up to about 600 feet. In fall 1964, a foursome including Robbins, Chuck Pratt, Yvon Chouinard, and Tom Frost took on the wall. After 10 days of storms, broken holds, tricky traverses, dwindling food supplies, and terrifying exposure, the team claimed the first ascent of this 2,400-foot, 28-pitch monster route. Robbins summed it up in describing one of the pitches just below the Igloo, a cave 300 feet below the top: “One of the hardest leads of my experience, it was just another pitch on this wall.”

Read this: “The First Ascent of the North America Wall” by Royal Robbins

With a relatively recent surge in slacklining, balance has become a common skill for climbers to practice on rest days. But 40 years ago, it wasn’t on anyone’s radar. Chuck Pratt is credited as the first Valley climber to train for balance. Here, he simultaneously tests his coordination by juggling.

Pratt was a Yosemite legend, with dozens of notable first ascents on formations like Fairview Dome in Tuolumne, Washington Column, the Salathé and North America Wall on El Capitan, the South Face of Mt. Watkins, and Arch Rock. Friend and partner Royal Robbins described him in a trip report about the first ascent of North America Wall: “Chuck’s fantastic native talents and unassuming demeanor make him the finest of climbing companions, while his infinite patience and sense of humor make him an excellent teacher and guide.”

Before guidebooks and apps, climbers passed around hand-drawn topos until they fell apart. This one mapped by the late Gary Colliver and Chris Jones informed an ascent of the Salathé Wall.

Warren Harding finishes the last pitch on the first ascent of the Dawn Wall on El Capitan after 28 days. Harding was nicknamed Batso for his ability to spend endless nights on the wall until the route was completed, as well as his boisterous personality. He bagged first ascents all over the Valley, including the Nose on El Cap, the North Face of the Rostrum, and the Direct Route of Lost Arrow Spire. A biopic entitled Batso about his life is currently in the works.

Read this: The Life of Warren “Batso” Harding by Burr Snider

Bill Westbay enjoys the comfort of a Navy surplus cot, the use of which started a trend of big wall climbers sleeping on flat, collapsible beds. These were the inspiration behind the current big waller’s bed, the portaledge.

This 50-foot crack climb just off Highway 120 first fell to the legendary Ron Kauk in 1978. It quickly became world-famous thanks to the wildly exposed and near-horizontal roof that comprises the second half of the route. Originally graded 5.12a, it was downgraded to 5.11d after a block broke off the lip, exposing a larger hold.

Eight years after the first ascent, the bold and super-strong German climber Wolfgang Güllich nabbed the first free solo after rehearsing it on a rope several times that same day. Other notable free soloists of the route include Alex Honnold, Dean Potter, and Heinz Zak. The latter did it in 2005, 19 years after photographing Güllich’s ropeless send. A quick hike from the car and a short rappel gets you down to the slabby staging area. But the moves over the lip put the climber out over some serious exposure. Here, Dave Diegelman uses jams and pre-placed gear while Bill Price belays.

California-climber poster boy John Bachar heads up the second pitch of Outer Limits (5.10c), a masterpiece first climbed in 1971 by Jim Bridwell and Jim Orey. With a perfect hand-sized crack and flaky holds on the edges, this route remains one of the best-loved climbs in the Valley. Belayed here by fellow Stonemaster Gib Lewis, Bachar later soloed this route in the 1980s. Around that same time, Bachar posted what would become an infamous character in Yosemite, offering $10,000 to any person who could follow him climbing for one full day. His reputation for dangerous routes and bold free solos preceded him—no one took the offer.

Read this: “Only Blasphemy” by John Long  about the time that Long tried to keep up with Bachar in J-Tree—and nearly died doing it.)

About 25 years before the iPod, Werner Braun rocks out while soloing Reed’s Pinnacle Direct, a popular ropeless ascent for the certified Yosemite hardman. Braun is known as being one of the longest-standing members of the esteemed Yosemite Search and Rescue (YOSAR), having served for more than 40 years. He’s also known for unofficially logging more ascents than anyone else of the popular and difficult Astroman, a 1,000-foot 5.11c on Washington Column. He also attempted to free climb The Nose in the early 1980s with Ron Kauk and Bev Johnson.

Four of Yosemite’s notorious pranksters goof off in the Valley: Werner Braun, Jim Pettigrew, Ron Kauk, and John Bachar (from left to right). Since the Stonemasters, climbers have helped define the culture of Camp 4 and beyond.
