#8166. “A Southern Storybook Brought to Life.” Inside South Carolina’s Luxurious Lowcountry 20,000-Acre Montage Palmetto Bluff.

(Photo: Top Left: Rebecca Norris; Bottom Left: Andrew Baldino; Right: Montage Palmetto Bluff)

Ever come across an incredible hotel that stops you mid-scroll and makes you think: Wow, wouldn’t it be something to stay there? We do, too—all the time. Welcome to Friday Fantasy, where we highlight amazing hotels, lodges, cabins, tents, campsites, and other places perched in perfect outdoor settings. Read on for the intel you need to book an upcoming adventure here. Or at least dream about it.

I’m traveling down a very narrow two-way road in a tinted Chevrolet Suburban when the chauffeur stops abruptly. He points out two alligators sunbathing on the rocks in the May River on our right. That is my first sighting of an alligator or any reptile in over 15 years—except for a strangely cute banana boa constrictor in my high school science class. I’m no fan of them.

That gator pair, and a few more, dot the river, alongside the long road leading up to Montage Palmetto Bluff, a five-star resort in South Carolina’s Lowcountry.

The sandy dirt road, shadowed by live oak trees draped in Spanish moss—a signature of the Lowcountry landscape—eventually opens onto the resort’s central property: a sprawling white mansion called the Main Inn.

After the driver helps unload my bags from the truck, resort staff greet me and lead me inside across the wide porch, a hallmark of any traditional Southern residence. The dark wooden floors creak under my feet, the same kind of creaking that reminds me of walking into the comfort of my grandma’s house.

Montage Palmetto Bluff is a 20,000-acre property tucked between Hilton Head Island and Savannah, Georgia. It has over 200 guest rooms, suites, cottages, and other residences, called Village Homes, Moreland Village Homes, and Signature Residences. (I stayed in one of the signature residences.)

The property also offers ample outdoor and wellness activities, including a shooting club, golf course, a 13,000-square-foot spa, a lawn and racquet club, and over 20 miles of walking and biking trails.

For folks who want to throw a lavish, intimate event or wedding, Palmetto Bluff features two beautiful chapels: the May River Chapel and the Somerset Chapel. The latter is where Justin Bieber and Hailey Baldwin held their wedding ceremony in 2019. Through the church’s arched windows, you’ll get magnificent views of the sunset.

The resort is approximately a 30-minute boat ride from Daufuskie Island, a remote, bridge-free barrier island between Hilton Head Island and Savannah, Georgia. It has white-sand beaches, one paved road on the less-developed side of the island, and a rich Gullah Geechee culture. The Gullah Geechee people are descendants of enslaved West Africans who were forced to work on plantations along the southeastern coast of the United States.

Despite the resort’s beauty, it sits atop a dark history. In the Antebellum Era, Palmetto Bluff was home to several plantations where enslaved people grew lucrative crops, including indigo, cotton, rice, corn, beans, and sweet potatoes.

“We believe it is important first and foremost to acknowledge the suffering endured by the enslaved individuals who lived and labored on this land,” Meghan Lamb, senior manager of marketing and public relations at Montage Palmetto Bluff, tells me. “These stories deserve to be shared openly and thoughtfully, both to honor those who came before us and to ensure their experiences, contributions, and enduring legacy are never forgotten,” she adds.

Lamb, who walked my fellow housemates and me through much of the property and, while sharing the Bluff’s rich history, also had an excellent eye for spotting gators.

As a Black person whose ancestors were enslaved on southern plantations, hearing about the history here was a painful reminder, but a lack of acknowledgment would have been even more so.

During the Civil War, Union troops captured the land, and many white families and enslaved people fled the area. Wealthy bankers and businesspeople later purchased the property, and the land changed hands several times. A banker named Richard T. Wilson bought the property in 1901, expanded it, had a large mansion built on the grounds, and gave the estate its current name: “Palmetto Bluff.” The mansion burned to the ground in a 1926 fire; the ruins remain preserved on the grounds today.

Palmetto Bluff is now owned by a private equity firm that specializes in resort management, Henderson Park and South Street Partners.

I stayed in one of the signature residences, houses available for rent for a period of time, with three others for four days and three nights.

The Signature Five Bedroom Lagoon Residence 1003 is a mansion with high ceilings and luxurious bathrooms, plus a fireplace, a porch, a separate cottage, and a large communal dining table nestled in the center of the home.

I chose the bedroom in the back left corner of the house; it had warm, yellow lighting, deep mahogany-colored walls, a king-sized bed, a lush en-suite bathroom, and some of the softest sheets I’ve laid my head on. Despite a packed schedule, I rested easy each night.

You can view room rates and book your stay at a signature residence here.

On my first night, we were welcomed with a Southern-style buffet in our signature residence. The menu was astounding: a traditional Lowcountry boil with shrimp, corn, potatoes, and sausage, plus fluffy biscuits, mac and cheese, collard greens, and peach cobbler for dessert.

There are also several places to dine across the property. Guests can indulge in fine Southern cuisine at the Octagon or at the elegant River House, which is where I ordered my first Wagyu steak. Brunch is served at Buffalos, and premium cocktails are available at Hush, a speakeasy. Along the lagoon waterway that runs through the resort is Fore & Aft, which serves delicious Mexican fare. Flame is a 1950s-vintage pizza truck you can easily walk up to and grab a slice in the evenings, Wednesday through Sunday. Buzz is a cozy cafe (I got a toasty ham-and-cheese croissant one morning that didn’t disappoint), and Melt is the Bluff’s ice cream parlor. The property even has its own gas station with a small grocery store.

For a fun treat, you can make your own s’mores at the massive fire pit behind the Main Inn every night at 9 P.M. I did, and it brought me back to when I used to make them as a kid by the campfire in my parents’ backyard.

As I mentioned—my schedule was packed, but I managed to fit in a few outdoor activities. The 20-plus miles of trails on Palmetto Bluff offer scenic walking and e-biking tours.

I had never been on an e-bike before, so I was pumped for this chance to do so on some beautiful trails. I liked that I could switch between regular biking and an electric boost to reach nearly 20 miles per hour. The combination of speed, wind in my hair, and stunning trail views was exhilarating, so much so that I even made the very risky decision to FaceTime my girlfriend with one hand to show her how much fun I was having.

Andrew Baldino, the public relations and marketing coordinator at Montage Palmetto Bluff, led the e-biking tour and pointed out spots most people tend to miss. One of those, he said, is River Road. The appeal? Sweeping live oaks, long Spanish moss, and extensive lush greenery, he tells me.

The Golden Hour E-Bike Excursion lasts for one hour and 15 minutes and costs $90 per person. You can book your slot here.

On the second day of my stay, I took a paint-and-sip class at my signature residence with renowned artist Amiri Farris, known for incorporating Gullah Geechee imagery into his work. We painted a blue crab because they’re often found in South Carolina estuaries, tidal creeks, salt marshes, and rivers.

On the third day, I embarked on the Daufuskie Island History Excursion tour. Because the tour lasts about four hours, you’ll need to book it early in the morning. My tour started at 7:30 A.M. It was one of the highlights of my trip. I saw dolphins along the way and learned about the island’s rich history on a golf-cart tour of the island’s untouched parts after hopping off the boat. Our captain, who steered the boat and led the golf-cart tour, made the experience even more worthwhile as he’s developed deep relationships with people on the island and shared stories about the island’s characters, bringing a humorous, jovial vibe to the trip.

Private tours for up to six people cost $895, tours for up to 12 people cost $1,195, and tours for up to 16 people cost $1,295. You can book them here.

I left my trip feeling nourished, calm, and more knowledgeable about the Lowcountry than before I arrived.

Lamb put it beautifully when I asked what about the Bluff makes visitors want to return—and even buy property on the resort: “It’s a Southern storybook brought to life.”

#8164. Search for One of the World’s Rarest Mushrooms on These Texas Trails

If it weren’t for Angel Schatz, the executive director at the Central Texas Mycological Society, I would have never spotted it. The dark brown lump of fungi was buried under leaf litter next to a blackened tree stump alongside Austin’s Shoal Creek Trail. Fortunately, locating fungi of all kinds is Schatz’s expertise. And as she led our group of mushroom-curious explorers into the trees, we all tittered with the excitement of spotting our first kirinomitake.

Known as the Devil’s Cigar—or Texas Star mushroom—this curious fungi is the official mushroom of the Lone Star State. While it has been spotted from Lubbock to Dallas and across the border in Oklahoma (plus in Japan and Taiwan), its small geographic range makes the Texas Star a rare find. In Central Texas, it thrives on decaying cedar elm stumps.

In addition to being geographically rare, these mushrooms tend to be exceptionally well camouflaged to their surroundings, especially in their cigar form––a dark brown bulbous lump often poking just an inch or two out of the soil with a tell-tale nipple on top. They’re inedible, but locate one that has spread open into its iconic star shape (when it releases its spores with an audible hiss), and it’s hard not to get excited.

Fortunately, there are plenty of trails in the region, especially in the Hill Country surrounding Austin and San Antonio, where you can spot this unique fungi.

To locate a Devil’s Cigar, head to areas where cedar elms grow in abundance. Scan the ground for old, black tree stumps, which mycologists refer to as “black crowns” for their blackened, multi-pointed shape.

Then, get low. You may not spot them at once, especially when grass is tall or leaf litter covers the ground. Brush away any foliage and loose dirt around the stump and you may find slightly fuzzy dark brown lumps or, if you’re lucky, a tan star. Many times, two or three mushrooms grow in close proximity.

The best time to find Devil’s Cigars in Texas is in the late fall through early spring when relative humidity is high, weather is more consistently moist, and overnight lows drop below 50°F. Head out after a rain and you’ll have an even better chance of finding them in their star form as additional moisture encourages them to crack open and send their spores flying. Once they do, you may have a week to spot them before they decompose or get nibbled by insects.

Want to find one for yourself? These trails offer a better-than-average opportunity.

Devils Backbone Trail, Inks Lake State Park, Burnet

This short but challenging trail leads you through woods with plenty of cedar elm, up rocky spines, and alongside a creek that feeds into the lake. A bird blind at one end offers the option to identify winged creatures as well as fungi.

Start this leisurely hike at the trailhead near Barton Springs Pool in Zilker Park near downtown Austin and head south along the Barton Creek Trail/Violet Crown Trail. Keep your eyes peeled for fungi as you hike to the 360 Trailhead, where you’ll turn around and retrace your steps.

Meander through live oak and cedar elm on this quiet stretch of trail on the southern edge of San Marcos. Start at the trailhead off Hunter Road and hike Dante’s Trail, which connects with Paraiso Trail to make a loop at the end.

#8160. 6 Ways to Score Free Ski Lift Tickets and Mountain Perks This Winter

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

This year, beat high lift ticket prices by volunteering as a patroller, adaptive ski instructor, or buy qualifying flight tickets to a number of select locations (Photo: South_agency/Getty Images)

With lift ticket prices regularly topping $250 across North American mountains, budget skiing takes strategy. Outside dug into this season’s best hacks for scoring free lift tickets for skiers and snowboarders, from airline promotions at nine marquee resorts, to volunteer opportunities, and even to going downhill with a U.S. Forest Service ranger.

This winter, we’re tracking the snowiest mountains in America and the rare super El Niño on the way. Now, here’s what you need to know for the 2026-27 winter season when it comes to snagging your free passes.

Located in the San Juan Mountains of Southwest Colorado, Purgatory Resort is a 30-minute drive from Durango. With over 1,600 acres and an average snowfall of 260 inches annually, the mountain offers a blend of steep tree skiing and open groomers.

During the 2026-27 season, Purgatory is offering skiers and snowboarders a free season pass in exchange for 14 days of volunteering. Four of those shifts must fall during peak season, including winter holidays, Presidents’ Day weekend, and spring break.

Several other mountains across the country offer similar incentives for those volunteering on the slopes. Winter Park Resort in Colorado, North Carolina’s Beech Mountain Resort, and Whiteface in New York all provide free lift tickets in exchange for volunteering on ski patrol or the safety team.

Alaska Airlines’ Atmos Rewards Alpine Getaways for the winter ski season lets passengers show a qualifying boarding pass at nine participating western U.S. and Canadian ski resorts for free lift tickets, rental upgrades, and resort discounts.

Eligible passengers flying into the following airports get a free full, same-day, or half-day ticket.

Jay Peak Resort in Vermont is celebrating its annual Day for the Devoted on November 27, 2026, featuring 750 free lift tickets

“Day for the Devoted opens the season with a thank you to the people who make this place what it is, and an invitation to anyone ready to become a part of it,” the resort writes on its website. You can register for the event here.

Buying a qualifying Helly Hansen ski jacket or pair of pants gets you a free day or a buy-one-get-one ticket at participating resorts across North America and Europe. Clothing must be from the latest Helly Hansen ski collection.

Buy your gear, find the resort you’d like to ski, and submit your receipt to redeem a pass. More information is available on the company website here.

Adaptive skiing nonprofits rely on volunteers to help people with disabilities experience skiing. In many cases, volunteers receive a complimentary lift ticket for the day they’re helping.

At Eagle Mountain Therapeutic Recreation in Showdown, Montana, volunteers 16 and older can receive free passes and lunches on the days they work. Those who work four events can receive a day pass to be used at any time, while those who commit to eight or more days will receive a free pass for the season, according to the program website.

The Outdoors for All at The Summit at Snoqualmie and Stevens Pass in Washington offers a variety of volunteer programs, from ski and snowboard instructors to support in snowshoeing and Nordic skiing. Full-time volunteers are eligible for a discounted season pass, while part-time volunteers receive a same-day lift ticket. All volunteers also receive ExpertVoice pro deals and have access to instructor development, adaptive teaching experience, and clinics.

Every Friday beginning January 30 through April 3, 2027, intermediate skiers and snowboarders can spend an hour skiing with a U.S. Forest Service (USFS) staff member through the Ski With a Ranger Tour. Attendance is first-come, first-served and limited to 12 participants daily.

Participants must provide their own lift ticket, but the program is part of a free conservation education initiative that shares the USFS mission in ski area management. Participants will also learn about natural resources and environmental stewardship, the USFS writes on its website.

Kelso Carapia, a recreation specialist with the USFS Lake Tahoe Basin Management Unit, has been leading the program for 14 years. She told Outside that participants can expect to learn about a host of topics, including water ecology, forest health, animals, survival strategies, fire management, general land stewardship, and the cultural and geological history of the Tahoe Basin.

Ski experience is necessary. The route is on intermediate and blue terrain only, and skiers will access at least two lifts as part of their tour.

“This is not a ski lesson,” Carapia said. “It is an interpretive tour. As much as we prioritize safety and comfort of our participants, we are not there to instruct.”

Heavenly Mountain Resort straddles the California-Nevada border in South Lake Tahoe, California, and Stateline, Nevada. With 4,800 skiable acres across four base areas, it’s also a major winter destination.

Ski With A Ranger tours are led by the United States Department of Agriculture’s Forest Service Conservation Education staff and volunteers through a cooperative effort between the Forest Service and Heavenly Mountain Resort.

#8158. The 10 Best Editor-Approved Black Friday Deals for Hikers

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Tent and boots (Photo: aire images / Moment via Getty)

The best parts of the outdoors are free—the soaring views, the rush of a snow-swollen creek, the feeling of dirt and pine duff under your soles. The gear to get there? Much less so. That’s why we appreciate holiday-season sales: Whether you’re shopping for yourself or someone else, it’s a chance to grab the equipment you need at a price that won’t leave you wincing. (That’s doubly true this year, with everything from shoes to sleep systems seemingly jumping in price.)

With Thanksgiving over, now is the time to grab some of the season’s best deals. We combed the outdoors’ best Black Friday sales in search of deals on Backpacker-tested and -approved gear, so you don’t have to worry about wasting your money. From an Editors’ Choice-winning tent to featherweight insulation, here’s what we found.

Another Editors’ Choice winner, the Blaze 60 is a lightweight pack that carries better than it has any right to. “You never really feel the pounds, even with north of 40 on board,” our reviewer said. A plastic framesheet, cushy padded hipbelt, and easy-to-adjust torso keep it feeling comfy under a load.

A fixed-length trekking pole in 2026? If you’re not using your poles to support a tent, it could make sense. The Distance Carbon removes the weight and complexity of an adjustment lock—a common failure point of adjustable models—to create a rigid, reliable pole ready for long days in the mountains.

If you’re looking for a bag upgrade, the Spark—a 1 lb, 1.4 oz model that’s warm enough for almost any above-freezing adventure—is a safe bet. Stuffed with 850-fill down, the Spark disappears into a pack, and a draft tube and baffles along the zipper help seal out the chill when it’s in use.

“Luxury” is a word we wouldn’t often apply to our backcountry sleep systems, but this one earns it. The 3.5-inch-thick Tensor Trail is plush for a one-pound pad, and our testers reported that its consistent baffles were exceptionally comfortable; on a trip to Michigan’s Isle Royale, reviewer Stephanie Pearson reported she fell asleep before sunset and ended up sleeping in the next morning.

Originally designed with alpinists in mind, Mountain Hardwear’s Ghost Whisperer line is perfect for anyone who likes to move fast. The 800-fill down insulation is warmer than the piece’s 8.3-ounce weight would suggest. Bonus: When not needed, it packs into its own pocket for easy stowage.

If the Ghost Whisperer’s selling point is its weight, the Helium’s is its durability. In our testing, the Helium survived crampon strikes and scrapes against rock and ice without visible harm. Nice touch: Fleece-lined hand pockets and deep internal pockets allow you to keep necessities close at hand.

An ultralight rain jacket is no good if it can’t, you know, keep out the rain. The Guardian Air delivers on both counts: At 7 ounces, it’s firmly on the featherweight side of the category, but its waterproofing is also head and shoulders above most competitors. In testing throughout Montana’s Bitterroot and Lolo National Forests, we found it shrugged off precip as well as far heavier models.

Radios make communication far easier during winter adventures, and we’ve yet to use a radio that we liked as much as the Rocky Talkie. With a range of up to 5 miles and a battery life of up to 5 days, its ready to go deep this winter.

The Tungsten UL 2 is a lightweight tent that doesn’t compromise: A freestanding design with dual doors and vestibules makes it simple to get in and out of and reliable in heavy weather, while pre-bent and color-coded clips make it easy to set up out of the box.

The Scarpa Rapid Mid GTX is one of my personal favorite hiking boots on the market, pairing a light 10.6-ounce weight with a Vibram MegaGrip outsole that can handle everything from the Utah desert to Appalachian peaks without wavering. A sock-like design hugs the foot, providing stability even on tricky scrambles.
